exam: Place the Alentejo as the broad inland south, a third of Portugal, hot and dry, and name the eight DOC sub-regions with Portalegre as the cool granite exception at altitude.
Give the red blend: Aragonez (Tempranillo), Trincadeira, Alicante Bouschet and Castelão, with Syrah and Touriga Nacional beside them.
Give the whites: Antão Vaz for body, Arinto for acidity, Roupeiro for aroma.
Know Alicante Bouschet as a French teinturier, red of flesh, that found its home here.
Define the talha and Vinho de Talha: clay vessel, skins in, opened on Saint Martin's Day, 11 November.
Separate Alentejo DOC (the eight sub-regions) from Vinho Regional Alentejano (the whole province).
Know the cork: the Alentejo's montado of cork oak, stripped every nine years at the least, supplies a large share of the world's wine corks.

grapes.name: Aragonez
grapes.styles: Tempranillo under its southern name: ripe red fruit and soft tannin, early ripening, the backbone of most Alentejo blends and a mainstay of the vineyard.

grapes.name: Trincadeira
grapes.styles: Spice, pepper and freshness when it ripens cleanly on the dry plain, where it is safer from the rot that plagues it elsewhere; Tinta Amarela in the north.

grapes.name: Alicante Bouschet
grapes.styles: The French teinturier bred in 1866, red of flesh and juice, that found its best home here: colour, tannin, dark fruit and longevity, the grape of the traditional estates.

grapes.name: Castelão
grapes.styles: Freshness and raspberry fruit in the sandier south, less important here than on the Setúbal sand.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.styles: Planted since the 1990s for perfume and structure in the ambitious reds, often with Syrah.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The international red that suits the heat best, ripe and peppery, in both the regional blends and single-varietal bottlings.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: A blending partner in the regional reds, ripening fully and easily on the plain.

grapes.name: Antão Vaz
grapes.styles: The Alentejo's own white, at home in Vidigueira: drought-tolerant, full, ripe tropical fruit and low acidity, so it is nearly always blended with Arinto and takes well to barrel.

grapes.name: Arinto
grapes.styles: The acid that survives the heat, blended with Antão Vaz and Roupeiro in almost every white.

grapes.name: Roupeiro
grapes.styles: An aromatic, early-drinking white, called Síria in the Beira Interior and Códega in the Douro, a traditional part of the white blend.

law.classification: DOC Alentejo, run by the Comissão Vitivinícola Regional Alentejana at Évora, is not one block but eight separate demarcated sub-regions scattered across the province: Portalegre, Borba, Redondo, Évora, Reguengos, Granja-Amareleja, Vidigueira and Moura. A wine may be labelled Alentejo DOC alone or with the sub-region's name, and it must come from the sub-region's land and recommended grapes. The DOC's grape list is its own and not a native one: a core group that must make at least three quarters of a blend, Aragonez, Trincadeira, Alicante Bouschet and Touriga Nacional with Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon beside them, under the ordinance of 2010 and its annex of 2014. Everything between the sub-regions, which is most of the Alentejo, is Vinho Regional Alentejano, the IGP, with a longer grape list, widened again in 2018, and looser rules; a great deal of the region's best wine carries it by choice. Vinho de Talha is a category within the DOC with its own rules on vessel, skins and date. Reserva and Garrafeira follow the national definitions. The old distinction between Alto and Baixo Alentejo, upper and lower, is geography and not law.
labels: The DOC: from one of the eight sub-regions.
The regional wine: from anywhere in the province.
The clay fermentation vessel; Vinho de Talha is the category.
The Alentejo's words for an estate and for the farmhouse on it; the quintas of the north are herdades here.
A vintage-dated wine with at least half a degree more alcohol than the regional minimum, usually oaked.
A red matured at least thirty months, twelve of them in bottle, with the Reserva margin of alcohol.
Old vines, often the mixed plantings of Portalegre.
The cork oak pasture that surrounds the vineyards and is protected by law.
tiers: DOC Alentejo
Wine from one of the eight demarcated sub-regions, with the DOC's core grapes (Syrah and Cabernet among them) at three quarters of the blend at the least; the sub-region's name may be added.
DOC Alentejo with a sub-region
Portalegre, Borba, Redondo, Évora, Reguengos, Granja-Amareleja, Vidigueira or Moura on the label: the whole wine from that sub-region.

Vinho
Wine with no origin claim.

made.viticulture: The Alentejo was a country of wheat, cork and sheep, and the vine was planted in earnest only from the 1980s, when the co-operatives were modernised and new estates were laid out on the plain in rows on wire, wide enough for machines, with drip irrigation from the start because a summer without rain allows nothing else. Irrigation is the region's defining choice: it keeps the vine alive and the yield steady, and the Alqueva reservoir has brought water to the hottest ground around Moura and Granja-Amareleja. Heat is the hazard, not rot; the canopy is managed for shade, picking begins in early August for the whites and runs through September, often at night to bring the fruit in cold, and the growers watch for sugar racing ahead of flavour and for acidity falling away. Portalegre is the exception that proves the rule: old bush vines on granite at six and seven hundred metres, mixed plantings of a dozen grapes picked together, rain from the mountain, a harvest weeks later than the plain and wines of real freshness. Cork oak stands in and around the vineyards everywhere; the montado is protected by law, the bark is stripped by hand once every nine years at the least, and the Alentejo is the heart of the world's cork production.
made.winemaking: The modern Alentejo red is made cleanly and ripely: destemmed, fermented in temperature-controlled stainless steel with pumping over, blended across grapes, aged in French and American oak barrels for the Reserva tier, bottled soft, and sold young. Alicante Bouschet brings the colour and tannin, Aragonez the flesh, Trincadeira the spice, Syrah the sweetness of fruit; the traditional estates still tread in stone lagares and age in large old wood for a longer-lived, tannic style. Whites are cold fermented and bottled early, with Antão Vaz sometimes fermented in barrel on its lees. Beside this stands a winemaking the Romans knew: the talha, a clay vessel of up to two thousand litres lined with pitch, in which destemmed grapes ferment with their skins, the cap punched down with a stick, the wine clarifying as the skins sink and settling under a seal of olive oil until it is opened on Saint Martin's Day, 11 November, and drawn from a tap at the base. The rules for Vinho de Talha DOC Alentejo, written into the appellation early in the 2010s, require the grapes to come from the sub-regions, the fermentation and the time on skins to pass in the talha, and the wine to stay there until that date. Vidigueira, with Vila de Frades, is the heartland, and a few co-operatives and many small cellars keep it.

places.name: Portalegre
places.note: The northernmost sub-region, on the granite of the Serra de São Mamede against the Spanish border, with vineyards at six to seven hundred metres and higher: cooler, wetter, picked weeks after the plain, with old mixed bush vines that give the Alentejo's freshest and most fragrant reds and whites. The exam's Alentejo exception.

places.name: Borba
places.note: The marble country north-east of Évora with Estremoz and Vila Viçosa, on clay and limestone with marble outcrops: firm, balanced reds from Aragonez and Trincadeira, and a co-operative founded in 1955 whose cork-labelled red is a national standard.

places.name: Estremoz
places.note: The marble town beside Borba, on the sub-region's northern edge, home to some of the plain's most serious family estates.

places.name: Redondo
places.note: South of Borba under the Serra d'Ossa, on schist and granite: ripe, generous reds, a strong co-operative and a tradition of clay talhas in the village cellars.

places.name: Évora
places.note: The sub-region around the Roman and university city at the centre of the province, on granite and clay: the site of the Cartuxa cellar, named for the Carthusian monastery beside it, and of the icon red named after a medieval wine of the city, Pêra-Manca.

places.name: Reguengos
places.note: Reguengos de Monsaraz, east of Évora towards the Alqueva lake and the fortified hill village of Monsaraz, on granite, schist and clay: the home of the estate that led the Alentejo's modern revival in the 1980s, and of a big co-operative.

places.name: Granja-Amareleja
places.note: The south-eastern sub-region near Moura, the hottest and driest ground in Portugal, on schist: concentrated, low-yield reds from old bush vines, now irrigated from the Alqueva.

places.name: Vidigueira
places.note: Below the Serra do Mendro fault, where the plain drops into the lower Alentejo: the warmest and earliest of the sub-regions but for the south-east, the home of Antão Vaz for whites, and with Vila de Frades the heartland of talha wine.

places.name: Vila de Frades
places.note: The village of the talhas, where clay vessels stand in the cellars and the wine is opened on Saint Martin's Day; the capital of Vinho de Talha.

places.name: Moura
places.note: The southernmost sub-region, on the Guadiana near the Alqueva dam, hot and dry on schist and limestone: full, ripe reds from Aragonez, Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet.

places.name: Alqueva
places.note: The reservoir on the Guadiana, filled from 2002 and one of the largest artificial lakes in western Europe, which brought irrigation to the dry south-east and water to Reguengos, Moura and Granja-Amareleja.

producers.name: Herdade do Mouchão
producers.why: The traditional Alentejo in one estate: Alicante Bouschet planted since the nineteenth century, trodden in stone lagares, aged in old wood, made to last decades.

producers.name: Herdade do Esporão
producers.why: The Reguengos estate whose winery of the 1980s led the Alentejo's modern revival and whose Reserva is one of the region's most widely known reds.

producers.name: Cartuxa, Fundação Eugénio de Almeida
producers.why: The Évora foundation that makes wine in a former Jesuit house beside the Carthusian monastery that named it, and bottles Pêra-Manca, the Alentejo's icon red, only in the years it judges fit.

producers.name: Adega de Borba
producers.why: The co-operative of the marble country, founded in 1955, whose cork-labelled Reserva taught a generation of Portuguese what an Alentejo red tastes like.

producers.name: Cortes de Cima
producers.why: A Vidigueira estate founded in 1988 that planted Syrah in the early 1990s, before the region's lists admitted it, and sold the wine unnamed as Incógnito; Syrah is on the Alentejo's lists now.

producers.name: Tapada do Chaves
producers.why: A Portalegre estate founded in 1901 with old mixed vineyards on the granite of São Mamede, the classic example of the mountain Alentejo.

producers.name: Adega Cooperativa de Vidigueira
producers.why: The co-operative of the talha heartland, which still ferments part of its wine in clay and is the easiest Vinho de Talha to find.

terroir.climate: Hot, dry and continental, among the hottest and driest ground on the mainland: summers above forty degrees are common, rainfall is low and falls in winter, and the south-east around Moura and Granja-Amareleja is the hottest, driest corner of Portugal. Nights cool the plain a little; altitude cools Portalegre a great deal, and the Serra de São Mamede brings it rain the plain never sees.
terroir.soils: A patchwork, poor and shallow almost everywhere: granite around Portalegre, Évora and Reguengos, schist across much of the south around Vidigueira and Moura, and the marble belt of Estremoz, Borba and Vila Viçosa with clay and limestone around it. In the south the heat matters more than the rock.
terroir.topography: Mostly a gently rolling peneplain between two and four hundred metres, broken by low ridges, the Serra d'Ossa behind Redondo and the Serra do Mendro, the fault scarp at Vidigueira that divides the upper Alentejo from the lower. The one true mountain is the Serra de São Mamede on the Spanish border, where Portalegre's vineyards climb to seven hundred metres and more.
terroir.water: The Guadiana runs south through the east of the region and feeds the Alqueva reservoir, filled from 2002 and among the largest artificial lakes in western Europe, which irrigates the vineyards of the dry south-east. Elsewhere the small rivers run dry in summer and irrigation draws on dams and wells.

traps: Aragonez is Tempranillo, the same grape as the Douro's Tinta Roriz; the Alentejo uses the southern name.
Alentejo on a label is the DOC from one of eight sub-regions; Alentejano is the regional wine from anywhere in the province.
Alicante Bouschet is a French crossing, not a Portuguese native, and one of the few red grapes with red juice.
Portalegre is not hot plain: it is granite at altitude in the Serra de São Mamede, picked weeks later, the freshest wine of the region.
A talha is a clay fermentation vessel, not a barrel; a lagar is the stone treading trough the traditional estates use.
Antão Vaz is the Alentejo's white; Arinto is blended in for acidity, Encruzado belongs to the Dão and Alvarinho to Vinho Verde.
Reguengos is Reguengos de Monsaraz; Monsaraz is the hill village, not a sub-region of its own.

wines.note: A blend of Aragonez, Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet, often with Syrah or Touriga: full, ripe, soft tannin, plum and dark cherry, a warm finish, a year in oak in the Reserva. The Alentejo's bread and butter, poured with grilled pork, lamb stew and the region's bread-and-garlic cooking.
The same grapes with the international ones from anywhere in the province, ripe and easy; much of the Alentejo's export volume carries this label.

Antão Vaz with Arinto and Roupeiro, sometimes Verdelho or Viognier: full, ripe, peach and citrus, best cold and young, some barrel-fermented for weight. It takes the region's fish soups and pork with clams.

Red, white or sometimes skin-contact white fermented and kept in clay talhas with the skins until Saint Martin's Day: rustic, textured, earthy and fresh, drawn from a tap at the base of the vessel. Serve cool with the cured meats and cheeses of the villages that make it.
From the granite slopes of the Serra de São Mamede, often old mixed vineyards: fresher, firmer and more fragrant than the plain's reds, picked weeks later, the Alentejo's claim to elegance.

exam: Name the grape, the soil and the climate together: Baga, clay-limestone, cool Atlantic.
Describe Baga: late, tight bunches, high acid, high tannin, tart cherry and tobacco, long-lived.
Know the second signature, traditional method sparkling wine, and its dish, leitão.
Know the date, 1979, the 2003 opening of the rules, and the Clássico label at 50 per cent Baga.
Name the whites: Bical, Maria Gomes (Fernão Pires), Arinto, Cercial.
Know the IGP, Beira Atlântico, and the place names Anadia and Mealhada.

grapes.name: Baga
grapes.styles: The grape of the region: small, thick-skinned berries in tight bunches, late ripening, high in acid and tannin, giving tart cherry, plum skin, tobacco and earth, hard when young and glorious at twenty years; also the base of rosé and blanc de noirs sparkling.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.styles: Allowed in the blend and welcome in a Clássico as a softener and perfume beside Baga.

grapes.name: Alfrocheiro
grapes.styles: A traditional partner that brings colour and soft fruit to a Baga blend.

grapes.name: Castelão
grapes.styles: A traditional variety of the sandier soils, fruity and supple, in blends.

grapes.name: Camarate
grapes.styles: An old local red of the traditional list, soft and early, for blends.

grapes.name: Maria Gomes
grapes.styles: Fernão Pires under its Bairrada name: aromatic, soft, early ripening, the base of much white and sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Bical
grapes.styles: The region's finest white, early and crisp, with citrus and a waxy texture that ages; the backbone of the best sparkling wines.

grapes.name: Arinto
grapes.styles: Acidity and lemon for the still and sparkling whites.

grapes.name: Cercial
grapes.styles: A high-acid white of the Beiras for the blends; not Madeira's Sercial.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Permitted since the rules opened, mostly for sparkling wine and for modern white blends.

law.classification: Bairrada was demarcated in 1979 and is DOC Bairrada under its regional commission, with Vinho Regional Beira Atlântico as the IGP around it. The rule book was rewritten in 2003: before it Baga was compulsory as the majority of every red; since then the DOC admits Touriga Nacional, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Pinot Noir beside the traditional grapes, and a wine with Baga at the centre may be labelled Bairrada Clássico, which requires at least 50 per cent Baga with the rest from the traditional list of Alfrocheiro, Camarate, Castelão, Jaen and Touriga Nacional. The whites rest on Maria Gomes, Bical, Arinto and Cercial. Sparkling wine is a category of the DOC in its own right, made by the traditional method, and the region carries the usual national terms, Reserva and Garrafeira.
labels: A Baga-led red of the traditional grapes.
Brut, the usual dryness of the sparkling wine.
The ageing term: thirty months with twelve in bottle on a red, which the old Baga wines exceed by years.
Own-rooted, ungrafted vines, possible on the sand.
Old vines, often Baga on the clay.
The regional wine of the coastal Beiras.
tiers: DOC Bairrada
The coastal plain demarcated in 1979: red, white, rosé and sparkling wine from the listed grapes, the reds since 2003 free to use international varieties.
Bairrada Clássico
The traditional red: at least 50 per cent Baga with the rest from Alfrocheiro, Camarate, Castelão, Jaen and Touriga Nacional.
Bairrada Espumante
Traditional method sparkling wine, white, rosé or blanc de noirs, the region's second signature.
Vinho Regional Beira Atlântico
The IGP of the coastal Beiras, for wines outside the DOC rules.

made.viticulture: Baga sets the terms. It buds early and ripens late, in October, with tight bunches of small, thick-skinned berries that rot in a wet autumn and never ripen if the vine is overcropped, so the whole art is getting the crop down and the canopy open: low cordons on wires, green harvesting, leaf pulling around the bunches, and a wait at the end of the season that can lose the year to rain. For most of the twentieth century the vineyard was planted for volume, Baga yielding hugely on the fertile clay and sold hard and thin, which is the origin of its rough reputation. The revival since the 1980s cut yields, picked riper, and chose sites: Baga on the clay-limestone for structure, lighter varieties and some Baga on the sand for finesse. Since 2003 Touriga Nacional, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Pinot Noir may be planted for the DOC, and some houses build their reds on them; the Clássico wines and the Baga specialists hold to the old grape. The sparkling houses pick early, in August and September, for acidity.
made.winemaking: The traditional red was fermented whole, stems and all, in open lagares or vats with long maceration, aged in large old casks of oak or chestnut and released tannic and acid to soften over ten or fifteen years. Modern Baga keeps the long life and loses the rawness: destemming or partial stems, cooler fermentation, softer extraction, a year or two in used French oak, and a late release. Sparkling wine has been made here since the 1890s and Bairrada was the first Portuguese region to be known for it: the traditional method, with the second fermentation in bottle and time on the lees, from Bical, Maria Gomes and Arinto for the whites and from Baga pressed quickly off its skins for the rosés and blancs de noirs. Some houses make a Baga rosé by a short maceration; a few make orange or amphora wines, but these are curiosities.

places.name: Anadia
places.note: The town at the centre of the region, home of the viticulture station founded in the nineteenth century and of the wine museum; the clay-limestone hills around it hold the classic Baga vineyards.

places.name: Mealhada
places.note: The town on the old Lisbon road famous for leitão à Bairrada, roast suckling pig served along a strip of restaurants, with the region's sparkling wine poured beside it; the clay of Mealhada also grows serious Baga.

places.name: Cantanhede
places.note: The western municipality towards the coast, sandier and lighter in its wines, with a large co-operative and the Baga on sand that teaches the soil lesson.

places.name: Buçaco and Luso
places.note: The forested hill on the eastern edge, with the spa town of Luso beneath it, whose palace hotel has blended and bottled its own long-aged Bairrada and Dão wines for over a century.

places.name: Sangalhos
places.note: A village near Anadia that houses the cellars of the region's largest sparkling and brand houses, built on the limestone for cool storage.

places.name: Águeda and Oliveira do Bairro
places.note: The northern municipalities towards the Vouga and the Aveiro lagoon, part of the sparkling trade and of the volume vineyard.

producers.name: Luís Pato
producers.why: The house that championed Baga from the 1980s, with single-vineyard wines from clay and an ungrafted planting on sand, and that led the region's revival.

producers.name: Caves São João
producers.why: The traditional house whose Frei João reds, released after years in cask, showed how long Baga could live.

producers.name: Casa de Saima
producers.why: A Sangalhos estate making Baga the old way, trodden in lagar and aged in old wood, a reference for the classic style.

producers.name: Quinta das Bágeiras
producers.why: A family estate near Anadia prized for serious Baga and for sparkling wine with long lees ageing.

producers.name: Caves Aliança
producers.why: The Sangalhos house of 1927 that made Bairrada sparkling wine a national habit and carries a wide range of Portuguese regions.

producers.name: Caves Messias
producers.why: A large Mealhada house of sparkling wine, Baga reds and aged aguardente.

producers.name: Campolargo
producers.why: The modern estate that planted international grapes beside Baga and makes the case for the 2003 rules.

producers.name: Buçaco Palace
producers.why: The hotel whose Bussaco reds and whites, blended from Bairrada and Dão and aged for years, are a collector's curiosity.

terroir.climate: Maritime and cool, the Atlantic twenty kilometres to the west and nothing in between to stop it: mild winters, warm rather than hot summers, sea fog and breezes, and rainfall around 1,000 millimetres with a share of it in autumn, which is Baga's trial, because the grape ripens late and its tight bunches rot in a wet October. The climate makes the acidity that the sparkling wines and the long-lived reds depend on.
terroir.soils: Heavy clay, the barro of the name, over limestone on the gentle rises: cold, water-holding, late-warming soils that suit Baga's structure. Towards the coast the soil turns to sand, which gives lighter, earlier reds and whites and, at one famous site, allowed ungrafted vines to survive. The clay-limestone and the sand are the region's two schools.
terroir.topography: Low and open: a plain and gentle hills between 40 and 120 metres, running south from the Vouga near Aveiro to the Mondego at Coimbra, with the Caramulo and the Buçaco hills rising to the east. Vineyards share the land with olives, maize and the pine of the dunes; there is nothing steep anywhere.
terroir.water: The Atlantic sets the climate, and the Ria de Aveiro lagoon to the north-west adds damp air. The Cértima, Bairrada's own small river, drains the plain into the Pateira de Fermentelos lagoon; the Vouga bounds the north and the Mondego the south. The spa waters of Luso and Curia are the other famous liquids of the region.

traps: Bairrada is clay and limestone on a flat coastal plain; the Dão next door is granite at altitude.
Baga is thin in colour when overcropped and black when yields are low; the grape is not the problem, the yield is.
Maria Gomes is Fernão Pires, not a separate grape; Cercial is not Madeira's Sercial.
Since 2003 a plain Bairrada red may contain no Baga at all; only Clássico guarantees it.
Bairrada's sparkling wine is traditional method, not tank method, and may be blanc de noirs from Baga.
Bairrada's date is 1979, not 1908: it is one of the newer demarcations.

wines.note: At least half Baga with the traditional grapes: deep ruby turning garnet, tart cherry and plum skin, tobacco, dried herbs and earth, high acid and drying tannin that need years in bottle. Decant it and serve with roast kid, game, or the leitão if the guest likes a red.
The modern blend after 2003, Baga softened with Touriga Nacional, Syrah or Merlot: rounder, earlier, oak-touched, and easier by the glass.

Traditional method sparkling wine, white from Bical, Maria Gomes and Arinto, or rosé and blanc de noirs from Baga, bone dry and high in acid; the classic match for leitão à Bairrada, the roast suckling pig of Mealhada.
Still whites from Bical, Maria Gomes and Arinto, crisp and lemony, some barrel fermented; good with the coast's fish and salt cod.
Pale, sharp rosés from Baga, drunk young and cold.
A smaller, finer-boned Baga from the sandy soils near the coast, including a famous ungrafted planting; lighter in colour, earlier to drink, a study wine for the sand against clay lesson.

exam: Place it: a granite plateau at 400 to 700 metres around Viseu, sheltered by the Caramulo and the Estrela, among pine forest.
Know the red grapes, Touriga Nacional, Jaen, Alfrocheiro and Tinta Roriz, and that Jaen is Mencía.
Encruzado is the white the exam wants placed here, and nowhere else.
Know the date, 1908, the seven sub-regions, and the IGP, Terras do Dão.
Know the story: co-operatives from the 1940s, revival after 1986 by estates.
Describe the style: fragrant, fresh, firm, medium bodied, long-lived.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.styles: Claimed as a native of the Dão, from the village of Tourigo near Tondela: here it is floral and fine-boned rather than massive, violets, bergamot and blackberry with firm, ripe tannin, in blends and as a varietal.

grapes.name: Jaen
grapes.styles: Galicia's Mencía under its Dão name: early ripening, red-fruited, supple and lower in tannin, the softener in a Dão blend and a pretty varietal.

grapes.name: Alfrocheiro
grapes.styles: Deeply coloured, soft and strawberry-scented, balancing Touriga's structure in the classic blend.

grapes.name: Tinta Roriz
grapes.styles: Tempranillo, adding fruit and body; it ripens early on the warmer slopes.

grapes.name: Rufete
grapes.styles: A light, high-acid red of the old mixed vineyards, more common towards the Spanish border.

grapes.name: Bastardo
grapes.styles: The Jura's Trousseau under a Portuguese name, pale and high in alcohol, a survivor in old plots.

grapes.name: Encruzado
grapes.styles: The region's great white and nearly its own: textured, mineral, citrus and fennel, takes barrel fermentation and lees like a white Burgundy and ages for ten years.

grapes.name: Bical
grapes.styles: An early, aromatic white shared with Bairrada, for blends and sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Cercial
grapes.styles: A high-acid white of the Beiras for freshness in blends; not Madeira's Sercial.

grapes.name: Malvasia Fina
grapes.styles: A soft, floral white in the traditional blends, called Boal in some places.

law.classification: The Dão was demarcated in 1908 and is DOC Dão under its regional commission, the CVR Dão, with Vinho Regional Terras do Dão as the IGP around it. The DOC names seven sub-regions that may appear on the label: Alva, Besteiros, Castendo, Serra da Estrela, Silgueiros, Terras de Azurara and Terras de Senhorim. Reds must be built on the recommended grapes, Touriga Nacional, Jaen, Alfrocheiro, Tinta Roriz, Rufete and their companions, and whites on Encruzado, Bical, Cercial, Malvasia Fina and Verdelho; varietal labels follow the national rule. A superior designation, Dão Nobre, exists for wines from the best fruit that meet stricter standards and longer ageing. The usual national terms apply: Reserva for a vintage and extra alcohol, Garrafeira for thirty months with twelve in bottle on a red.
labels: A vintage and half a degree more alcohol than the minimum, as across Portugal.
The ageing term: thirty months with twelve in bottle for a red.
Old vines, usually the mixed plots of the pre-revival vineyard.
The regional wine of the plateau.
tiers: DOC Dão
The whole plateau demarcated in 1908: reds, whites, rosés and sparkling wines from the region's grapes under the CVR Dão.
Dão with a sub-region
One of the seven sub-regions on the label: Alva, Besteiros, Castendo, Serra da Estrela, Silgueiros, Terras de Azurara or Terras de Senhorim.
Dão Nobre
The superior designation for wines meeting stricter grape, alcohol and ageing standards.
Vinho Regional Terras do Dão
The IGP of the same land, for wines outside the DOC list.

made.viticulture: The Dão vineyard is a patchwork. Holdings are small, walled in granite and scattered through the pine forest, often old mixed plantings of a dozen varieties on bush vines or low cordons; the modern estates plant blocks of Touriga Nacional, Jaen, Alfrocheiro and Encruzado on wire-trained vines. Altitude sets the season: budbreak is late enough to dodge most spring frost, summers are dry, and harvest runs from late September into October with the Estrela already cold at night. Poor granite sand keeps yields modest without much help. The hazards are fire in the summer forest and drought in a hot year rather than rot. The region's history is written in its vineyards too: from the 1940s until the end of the 1980s the law channelled growers' grapes into co-operatives, which made the Dão a byword for hard, dull red; after Portugal joined the European Community the estates took back their fruit, and the finest old plots at altitude, in Silgueiros, Senhorim and under the Estrela, became the raw material of the revival.
made.winemaking: Traditional Dão red was fermented with stems in open stone lagares or old wooden vats, left long on its skins, aged for years in large old casks of oak or chestnut and sold firm and dried out. The revival kept the structure and lost the harshness: destemming, gentler extraction in stainless steel or lagar, moderate time in French oak of various sizes, and bottling while the fruit still shows. Many houses keep the old habit of blending four or five grapes, because Touriga Nacional alone can be too austere young and Jaen too soft. Encruzado is the white that justified barrel fermentation in Portugal: whole-bunch pressing, fermentation in oak, lees stirring and a year in wood give a wine of texture and length, though stainless steel versions keep the grape's citrus edge. Sparkling wine is made by the traditional method with a second fermentation in bottle.

places.name: Viseu
places.note: The cathedral city at the centre of the plateau, the seat of the regional commission and the hub from which the sub-regions radiate.

places.name: Silgueiros
places.note: The sub-region south of Viseu along the Dão river, prized for Encruzado and for fine, fragrant reds; many of the revival's single-estate wines come from here.

places.name: Terras de Senhorim
places.note: Around Nelas and Canas de Senhorim in the heart of the plateau, home of the historic manors of Santar and of some of the oldest estates to bottle their own wine.

places.name: Terras de Azurara
places.note: Around Mangualde east of Viseu, with several of the leading modern estates and a reputation for Touriga Nacional.

places.name: Serra da Estrela
places.note: The highest sub-region under the mountains in the south-east, around Seia and Gouveia, with the coolest sites, old vines and the longest, freshest reds; the sheep's cheese of the same name is the region's great table match.

places.name: Besteiros
places.note: The western sub-region at the foot of the Caramulo around Tondela, nearest the Atlantic weather and the claimed cradle of Touriga Nacional at Tourigo.

places.name: Castendo and Alva
places.note: Castendo lies in the north-east around Penalva do Castelo; Alva in the south along its river towards Oliveira do Hospital. Both are small and rarely named on a label.

places.name: Santar
places.note: A village of granite manor houses near Nelas whose estates have bottled Dão under their own names for generations, a landmark of the region's revival.

producers.name: Quinta dos Roques
producers.why: A Mangualde estate whose varietal Touriga Nacional and barrel-fermented Encruzado defined the modern Dão in the 1990s.

producers.name: Quinta da Pellada
producers.why: An old-vine estate under the Serra da Estrela at Seia, with its sister Quinta de Saes, a reference for fine, ageworthy Dão red.

producers.name: Quinta dos Carvalhais
producers.why: The Dão estate of the Sogrape group at Mangualde, widely poured abroad, with a dependable Encruzado.

producers.name: Casa de Santar
producers.why: The historic manor of Santar near Nelas, among the first houses to bottle estate Dão and still a name a guest may know.

producers.name: Casa da Passarella
producers.why: A nineteenth-century estate at Gouveia under the Estrela, revived with old vines and a classical style.

producers.name: Quinta de Cabriz
producers.why: The large Carregal do Sal estate whose reliable reds put Dão by the glass on lists everywhere.

producers.name: Caves São João
producers.why: The Bairrada house whose Porta dos Cavaleiros label kept long-aged traditional Dão alive through the co-operative decades.

terroir.climate: Temperate and sheltered. Rain is plentiful, around 1,100 millimetres, but falls mostly in winter; summers are warm and dry, with days in the mid thirties and cool nights that the altitude guarantees. The Caramulo and Buçaco hills to the west take the Atlantic weather, the Estrela to the south-east holds off the continental heat and gives spring snowmelt. The result is a slow, even ripening season and reds with freshness that the hotter Douro lacks.
terroir.soils: Granite, weathered into coarse sand the growers call saibro, poor, acidic and free draining, lying over bedrock that forces roots to search. A little schist appears at the southern and western margins. The low fertility holds yields down naturally and the sand keeps the wines fine-boned rather than heavy.
terroir.topography: A high, undulating plateau at 400 to 700 metres, rising towards the Serra da Estrela, Portugal's highest mainland range, in the south-east and dropping towards the Mondego valley. The vineyards are small, walled plots scattered among maritime pine, eucalyptus and granite boulders, never a continuous carpet; the forest shelters them and scents the air.
terroir.water: Three rivers name the region's parts: the Dão itself, which gives the region its name, the Mondego, the longest river entirely within Portugal, which runs south-west through the plateau to Coimbra, and the Alva in the south. Their valleys are the warmer, lower sites; the rivers matter more for the landscape than for the climate.

traps: Dão is granite, like Vinho Verde, not schist like the Douro; the climate is the difference between those two granites.
Jaen is Mencía, not a Spanish town's wine; the name is the same as the Andalusian city but the grape is Galician.
Encruzado belongs to the Dão; Arinto is Bucelas and Vinho Verde, Antão Vaz is the Alentejo, Bical is shared with Bairrada.
Touriga Nacional is claimed by the Dão, not the Douro, as its birthplace.
The Dão lies south of the Douro and east of Bairrada, inland; it is not on the coast.
Cercial of the Dão and Bairrada is not Madeira's Sercial.

wines.note: The classic blend of Touriga Nacional, Jaen, Alfrocheiro and Tinta Roriz: medium bodied, fragrant, red and black fruit with pine and earth, fresh acidity and firm, fine tannin, built to age ten or twenty years. Roast kid, lamb and the region's cured meats are its table.
The varietal: violets, bergamot and blackberry with the plateau's freshness, more perfume and less weight than its Douro cousin.
Often barrel fermented and lees aged: textured, citrus and white flowers over wet stone and a hint of fennel, able to age a decade; roast chicken, grilled fish, pork with clams.
Blends of Encruzado, Bical, Cercial and Malvasia Fina, crisp and clean when young, the everyday white of Viseu's tables.
Traditional method sparkling wine from the high, cool vineyards, from Encruzado, Bical and Touriga Nacional; a small category with real acidity.
Pale rosés from Touriga Nacional and Jaen, dry and fresh, for the summer.

exam: Hold the two families apart: Ruby (fruit, bottle, decant) against Tawny (air, wood, no decanting), and place Vintage, LBV, Crusted and Colheita on the right side.
Know the fortification numbers: 77 per cent spirit, about one part in five, 19 to 22 per cent finished, the ferment stopped at roughly half the sugar.
Know the three sub-regions in order upstream and their characters, with Pinhão at the heart of the Cima Corgo.
Name the five favoured grapes and which is the most planted (Touriga Franca).
The dates: 1703 Methuen, 1756 demarcation, 1933 the institute, 1952 Barca Velha, 1982 DOC Douro, 1986 shipping from the Douro, 2001 World Heritage.
Know the LBV and Vintage bottling windows and the seven years of a Colheita.
Know what the cadastro and the beneficio are and why a grade matters.
Service: decant Vintage and Crusted and unfiltered LBV; pour aged tawny cool; White Port cold.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.styles: Small berries, thick skins, low yields: violets, bergamot, blackberry, deep colour and firm tannin, the grape that structures a Port blend and leads the best dry reds.

grapes.name: Touriga Franca
grapes.styles: The most planted grape of the Douro, late ripening and reliable on hot sites, floral and juicy, the flesh and the perfume of the blend.

grapes.name: Tinta Roriz
grapes.styles: Tempranillo under its Douro name, Aragonez further south: generous fruit and body, early ripening, best on cooler sites.

grapes.name: Tinta Barroca
grapes.styles: Early ripening and high in sugar, soft and fleshy, planted on cooler, higher or north-facing land so that it keeps its balance.

grapes.name: Tinto Cão
grapes.styles: Low yielding and late, fine-boned with good acidity and long life, prized in small measure for the blend's spine.

grapes.name: Sousão
grapes.styles: A teinturier with red flesh, the Vinhão of Vinho Verde: colour and acidity for Port in a hot year.

grapes.name: Tinta Amarela
grapes.styles: Trincadeira in the south: spicy and aromatic, rot-prone on the coast but at ease in the dry Douro.

grapes.name: Gouveio
grapes.styles: Godello of Galicia: the backbone of the Douro's dry whites and the base of White Port, with Malvasia Fina, Rabigato and Viosinho.

grapes.name: Rabigato
grapes.styles: A high-acid white of the Douro Superior that keeps the dry whites fresh.

grapes.name: Viosinho
grapes.styles: A low-yielding, aromatic white used for the best dry whites from altitude.

grapes.name: Moscatel Galego
grapes.styles: The small-berried Muscat, grown on the Favaios plateau above Pinhão for the fortified Moscatel do Douro.

law.classification: In 1756 the Marquis of Pombal demarcated the Douro and gave the Companhia Geral da Agricultura das Vinhas do Alto Douro charge of its trade. Port's institute was founded in 1933 and became the IVDP, the Instituto dos Vinhos do Douro e do Porto, in 2003; it regulates both DOC Porto and DOC Douro, the dry wine appellation of 1982, with Vinho Regional Duriense as the IGP. Port's categories are defined by the IVDP: Ruby, Reserve, LBV (bottled between the fourth and sixth year after harvest), Crusted (unfiltered, three years in bottle), Vintage (a declared year, bottled in its second or third year), Tawny, Reserve Tawny, tawny with an indication of age (10, 20, 30, 40 and since 2022 50 Years), Colheita (one harvest, at least seven years in wood), White, Rosé and Garrafeira. Port must be made within the region and, since 1986, may be aged and shipped from the Douro as well as from Gaia.
labels: An estate; a single quinta Port comes from one farm, often in an undeclared year.
A house's decision, approved by the IVDP, that a year is good enough for a Vintage Port; roughly three years in ten.
A single-harvest tawny, at least seven years in wood, with its bottling date.
10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 Years on a tawny or white: the blend's average age and style, not a vintage.
An LBV that spent at least three years in bottle before release, the unfiltered style.
Old vines, usually a mixed field blend on the old terraces.
The annual licence to fortify, shared out by vineyard grade.
The vineyard register that grades each plot by letter, A the best.
The warehouse where Port ages, traditionally in Vila Nova de Gaia.
The Port cask, around 550 litres in the Douro, and the unit the trade counts in.
tiers: DOC Porto
Fortified wine of the demarcated Douro, 19 to 22 per cent, made from grapes graded in the cadastro and fortified within the beneficio; the categories above.
DOC Douro
The dry wines of the same region since 1982: red, white and rosé, plus Moscatel do Douro; Barca Velha of 1952 is the ancestor.
Vinho Regional Duriense
The IGP of the valley, for wines that step outside the DOC grape list or rules.
Ruby family
Ruby, Reserve Ruby, LBV, Crusted, Vintage and Single Quinta Vintage: wine kept from air so that it stays red and fruity, the best of it aged in bottle and decanted.
Tawny family
Tawny, Reserve Tawny, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 Years, Colheita: wine aged in wood with air so that it turns amber and nutty, ready when bottled, never decanted.
The three sub-regions
Baixo Corgo, the wettest and most fertile; Cima Corgo around Pinhão, the heart and the home of the great quintas; Douro Superior, the driest and hottest, up to the Spanish border.

made.viticulture: Every Douro vineyard carries a grade. The cadastro, the vineyard register, scores each plot on altitude, locality, slope, aspect, soil, shelter, vine age, density, yield and grape varieties, and ranks it by letter from A, the best, downward. Each year the IVDP sets the beneficio, the volume of must that may be fortified, and shares it out by grade, so a top plot may turn most of its crop into Port while a poor one sends its grapes to DOC Douro or the regional wine. The terraces tell the region's history: the walled socalcos of the pre-phylloxera vineyard, some abandoned as mortórios after the louse arrived in the 1860s; the bulldozed patamares of the replanting that began in the 1970s; and vinha ao alto, rows straight up the gentler slopes. The old vineyards are mixed field blends of dozens of varieties; the new ones are blocks of the five favoured grapes, Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca and Tinto Cão, chosen by research in the 1970s and 1980s. Yields are low, heat and drought are the hazards, picking is by hand from mid-September, and the highest land is now planted for whites and freshness.
made.winemaking: Port is made fast. Because fermentation will be stopped after two or three days, colour and tannin must come out quickly, and the valley found ways to do it: foot treading in shallow granite lagares, robotic lagares, autovinifiers and pumping over. When the must has fermented roughly half its sugar, at about six to nine per cent alcohol, it is run off the skins into a vat holding aguardente, grape spirit at 77 per cent, near one part spirit to four of wine. The yeast dies, the sugar stays, and the Port finishes at 19 to 22 per cent with the sweetness of its own grapes. From then on it is a matter of air and time: Ruby, LBV and Vintage are kept in large vats or bottled early to hold their colour, while tawnies live in pipes of around 550 litres in the lodges of Gaia or, since 1986, in the Douro itself, where the heat speeds the ageing. Dry Douro wines ferment to completion, mostly in stainless steel or lagares, and age in French oak; the whites from altitude are often barrel fermented.

places.name: Baixo Corgo
places.note: The western, downstream sub-region around Peso da Régua, the old river port and administrative town, below the mouth of the Corgo: the wettest and coolest, the most fertile and the highest yielding, the source of much basic Ruby and Tawny and of good dry wine from its higher slopes.

places.name: Cima Corgo
places.note: The central sub-region upstream of the Corgo, centred on Pinhão: steeper, hotter and drier than the Baixo Corgo, home of most of the famous quintas and of the bulk of Vintage Port.

places.name: Pinhão
places.note: The small town at the Pinhão river's mouth whose railway station is tiled with vintage scenes; the great quintas of the shipping houses, Noval and Crasto lie around it on both banks.

places.name: Vale de Mendiz
places.note: A village of old field-blend vineyards above Pinhão, the source of some of the Douro's most celebrated dry reds.

places.name: Douro Superior
places.note: The eastern sub-region from the Valeira gorge to the Spanish border at Barca d'Alva: the hottest, driest and most recently planted, with gentler slopes near the river, the source of Barca Velha and Quinta do Vale Meão.

places.name: Quinta de Vargellas
places.note: A Taylor's estate since 1893, far upriver where the Cima Corgo gives way to the Douro Superior, famous for its single quinta Vintage Port.

places.name: Vila Nova de Gaia
places.note: The town across the river from Porto where the shippers' lodges stand and where by law all Port was aged and shipped until 1986; the names on the roofs are still the houses a guest knows.

places.name: Porto
places.note: The city at the river's mouth that gave the wine its name, Oporto in old English usage; the British shippers' Factory House dates from 1790 and the Port Wine Institute began here in 1933.

producers.name: Taylor Fladgate
producers.why: Founded in 1692, owner of Quinta de Vargellas, maker of the first commercial LBV with its 1965 vintage released in 1970, and a benchmark for firm, long-lived Vintage Port.

producers.name: Fonseca
producers.why: A house of 1815 in the same group as Taylor's, famous for a richer, more opulent Vintage style and for Bin 27 as the Reserve Ruby everyone knows.

producers.name: W. and J. Graham's
producers.why: Founded in 1820 and built on Quinta dos Malvedos since 1890, known for a sweet, generous Vintage style and for its 20 Years tawny.

producers.name: Dow's
producers.why: The driest of the great Vintage styles, built on Quinta do Bomfim at Pinhão and Senhora da Ribeira upstream.

producers.name: Warre's
producers.why: The oldest of the British houses, trading since 1670, with Quinta da Cavadinha and a traditional unfiltered LBV.

producers.name: Niepoort
producers.why: A family house of 1842 famous for Colheitas, for the cask-then-demijohn Garrafeira style and, since the 1990s, for the dry Douro reds that changed the valley's ambitions.

producers.name: Sandeman
producers.why: Founded in 1790, with the caped Don silhouette of 1928 that made it the most recognisable label in Port, strong in LBV and aged tawny.

producers.name: Feist
producers.why: A small nineteenth-century shipper whose long-matured LBVs give a taste of mature Port at a modest price.

producers.name: Quinta do Noval
producers.why: The Pinhão estate whose 1931 made its name and whose Nacional, from a tiny plot of ungrafted vines, is the rarest Vintage Port of all.

producers.name: Casa Ferreirinha
producers.why: The dry-wine house of Ferreira, founded 1751, and the maker of Barca Velha, the first great Douro table wine, from 1952.

producers.name: Quinta do Crasto
producers.why: A Cima Corgo estate between Régua and Pinhão whose single-vineyard old-vine reds, Maria Teresa and Vinha da Ponte, are reference dry Douro.

producers.name: Quinta do Vallado
producers.why: A Baixo Corgo estate near Régua dating from 1716, linked to the Ferreira family, known for dry reds and aged tawnies.

producers.name: Quinta do Vale Meão
producers.why: The Douro Superior estate built by Dona Antónia Adelaide Ferreira in the 1880s, the source of Barca Velha's grapes for decades and of its own great red since 1999.

producers.name: Wine and Soul
producers.why: A Vale de Mendiz house whose Pintas, from an old field blend, is a modern icon of dry Douro.

producers.name: Croft
producers.why: One of the oldest names in the trade, maker of Quinta da Roêda vintage Ports and the first Rosé Port in 2008.

producers.name: Ramos Pinto
producers.why: A Portuguese house of 1880 known for aged tawnies and for the research that chose the Douro's five favoured grapes.

producers.name: Kopke
producers.why: The oldest Port house, dating from 1638, and a specialist in Colheitas and very old tawnies.

terroir.climate: Continental with a Mediterranean summer. The Serra do Marão takes the Atlantic rain, so rainfall falls from around 900 millimetres in the Baixo Corgo to under 400 in the Douro Superior, while summer temperatures pass 40 degrees in the gorge and winters are cold. Altitude moderates: the valley floor is hottest and the vineyards climb to 700 metres, where whites and fresher reds now go. Drought and heat, not rot, are the hazards.
terroir.soils: Schist, xisto, a laminated metamorphic rock that splits into near-vertical plates, so roots follow the fissures many metres down to water. It is poor in nutrients, holds the day's heat and gives it back at night. Granite outcrops at the region's edges and on the higher ground, and the vineyard register marks it down, because granite holds less water and makes lighter wine.
terroir.topography: A steep, winding gorge: slopes of 30 degrees are ordinary and some pass 60, which is why the vineyard is terraced. The old socalcos are narrow walled steps built by hand before phylloxera; patamares are the wide bulldozed terraces of the 1970s onward that let a tractor through; vinha ao alto plants rows straight up the gentler slopes. The south-facing north bank is hotter, and every side valley has its own climate.
terroir.water: The Douro rises in Spain as the Duero, forms the border for some way, leaves it at Barca d'Alva at the eastern end of the Douro Superior and runs west for around two hundred kilometres to Porto. The Corgo divides the Baixo Corgo from the Cima Corgo, the Pinhão valley is the heart of the Cima Corgo, and the Cachão da Valeira gorge marks the start of the Douro Superior. The Tua, Torto, Távora, Sabor and Côa are other tributaries a label may name.

traps: Colheita and Vintage are both single-year Ports, but Colheita is a wood-aged tawny and Vintage a bottle-aged ruby: opposite wines.
A tawny's 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 Years is an average-age indication, never a vintage; Colheita is the vintage-dated tawny.
Port is sweet from its own grape sugar, stopped by spirit; nothing is added to sweeten it.
Vintage Port is bottled young, in its second or third year; LBV is bottled later, in its fourth to sixth, which is what Late means.
The most planted grape is Touriga Franca, not Touriga Nacional, however often the latter is named first.
Tinta Roriz is Tempranillo; Sousão is Vinhão; Gouveio is Godello; Tinta Amarela is Trincadeira.
Vila Nova de Gaia is where Port is aged, not where its grapes grow; the vineyard lies about 100 kilometres (sixty miles) upstream behind the Marão.
Douro Superior means upstream and inland, towards Spain, the driest end of the valley, not a superior grade.

wines.note: Young, deep red and fruity, a blend of years kept two or three years in large vats and filtered; serve slightly cool with chocolate, blue cheese or a berry dessert. Reserve Ruby is the richer selection.

A single year, kept four to six years in wood and bottled ready to drink, usually filtered so that it needs no decanting; the traditional unfiltered kind throws a deposit and is decanted. Ripe plum and spice at a fraction of a Vintage's price.

The top of the Ruby family: one declared year, bottled unfiltered in its second or third year, then matured for decades in bottle, where it throws a crust. Decant it. Black fruit, violets, firm tannin; Stilton and walnuts are the classic table.
A Vintage Port from one estate, such as Vargellas or Bomfim, often released in the years a house does not declare, and served exactly like a Vintage Port.
Aged in pipes with a little air, so the colour fades to amber and the fruit turns to nuts, dried fig and caramel; a Reserve has real age. Serve cool with crème brûlée, pecan pie or hard cheese.

10, 20, 30 or 40 Years, and since 2022 also 50 Years: the number is an indication of the blend's average age and character, approved by the IVDP's tasting panel, not the age of any one wine. Twenty is the sommelier's sweet spot: walnut, orange peel, toffee.
wines.style: Tawny with an Indication of Age

wines.note: A tawny from one harvest, aged at least seven years in wood and often far longer, bottled when sold with the bottling date on the label. Single-vintage like a Vintage Port but opposite in character: oxidative, amber, nutty, ready on opening.
From Gouveio, Malvasia Fina, Rabigato and Viosinho, dry to sweet, Lágrima the sweetest; aged whites carry the same indications of age. Served cold, often with tonic and mint as the Douro's aperitif.

Dry wines from the Port grapes, often old-vine field blends: dark, structured, schist-scented, with French oak; the best, from Barca Velha onward, age for decades and sit with lamb, game and grilled meats.
From Gouveio, Rabigato, Viosinho and Arinto grown at altitude: stony, textured, sometimes barrel fermented, and the valley's answer to white Burgundy.

exam: Know the former name, Estremadura, and that Lisboa is a Vinho Regional with nine DOCs inside it.
Place the three historic DOCs and their styles: Bucelas (Arinto white), Colares (own-rooted Ramisco on sand), Carcavelos (fortified).
Know Bucelas's rule, at least 75 per cent Arinto, white only.
Know why Colares vines are ungrafted: phylloxera cannot live in sand.
Know Alenquer and Montejunto as the serious red country, and Lourinhã as the brandy appellation.
Name the grapes: Arinto, Fernão Pires, Vital; Castelão, Aragonez, Touriga Nacional, Syrah.

grapes.name: Arinto
grapes.styles: The grape of Bucelas: crisp, lemony, mineral whites that keep their acidity in the heat and age into something nutty; also sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Fernão Pires
grapes.styles: The aromatic, soft white that fills the regional blends and the sparkling wines of Óbidos.

grapes.name: Vital
grapes.styles: A neutral local white of the volume vineyards around Torres Vedras and Alenquer.

grapes.name: Malvasia
grapes.styles: Malvasia de Colares makes the rare white of Colares, salty and waxy from the sand.

grapes.name: Ramisco
grapes.styles: The red grape of Colares, grown nowhere else, own-rooted in sand: pale, tannic, high in acid, long-lived and austere, a wine of the past that still exists.

grapes.name: Castelão
grapes.styles: The region's traditional red, also called Periquita: raspberry, leather and supple tannin, happiest on sand and warm clay.

grapes.name: Aragonez
grapes.styles: Tempranillo under its southern name, giving body and fruit to the Alenquer and regional reds.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.styles: Perfume and structure for the Alenquer blends.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The international grape that found a home in Alenquer's shelter, making peppery, polished reds.

grapes.name: Tinta Miúda
grapes.styles: Graciano of Rioja under a Portuguese name, an old local variety for acidity and colour in Alenquer blends.

grapes.name: Alicante Bouschet
grapes.styles: The teinturier that gives colour to some of the regional reds.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Planted by the modern estates of Alenquer for blends.

law.classification: Lisboa is the Vinho Regional, the IGP, that covers the coast north of the capital, renamed from Estremadura so that the wine carried the city's name. Inside it lie nine DOCs: Alenquer, Arruda, Bucelas, Carcavelos, Colares, Encostas d'Aire, Lourinhã, Óbidos and Torres Vedras. Three are among the oldest in Portugal: Carcavelos and Colares were demarcated in 1908 and Bucelas in 1911. Bucelas is a white DOC only, with at least 75 per cent Arinto. Colares requires Ramisco to lead its red and Malvasia de Colares its white, from the sand. Carcavelos is a fortified wine. Lourinhã is an appellation for aguardente, grape brandy alone, a rarity it shares with Cognac and Armagnac. The other DOCs are small and little used, so most of the region's wine is sold as Vinho Regional Lisboa, which permits a long list of native and international grapes.
labels: The regional wine; the word on most of the labels.
The former name of the regional wine, still seen on older bottles.
Sand ground and hard ground: the two soils of Colares, only the first within the DOC's sand rule.
Own-rooted, ungrafted vines, as at Colares.
A brand name that became a synonym for Castelão.
Grape brandy, the product of DOC Lourinhã.

DOC Bucelas
White only, at least 75 per cent Arinto, from the Trancão valley north of Lisbon; demarcated 1911.

An appellation for aguardente, grape brandy, not for wine.

made.viticulture: Wind is the first fact: vines are trained low, hedges and walls are planted as breaks, and the coastal sites choose early grapes. Colares is the extreme. Its vines are planted in trenches dug through the dune to the clay beneath and the sand filled back as they grow, so the roots sit in clay and the trunks in sand where phylloxera cannot follow; the canes are trained along the ground, the bunches lifted on props, and reed fences shelter the rows from the salt wind. Bucelas grows Arinto on the limestone slopes of the Trancão valley north of the city. Alenquer, east of Montejunto, is wire-trained and modern, with south-facing slopes that ripen Touriga Nacional and Syrah. Torres Vedras and Arruda hold the mechanised volume vineyards that feed the regional wine and once fed the bulk trade. Harvest runs from late August for the sparkling and the whites into late September for the reds. The historic DOCs face a hazard no spray can treat: the city's spread, which has reduced Carcavelos to a handful of hectares and Colares to a fraction of its former vineyard.
made.winemaking: Bucelas is made as a modern dry white, cold fermented in stainless steel, sometimes with lees contact, and a part of it as traditional method sparkling. Colares keeps the old way: Ramisco fermented on its skins, aged for years in large old wooden vats at the Adega Regional de Colares, the co-operative founded in 1931, and released mature, with a few private houses holding stocks that go back decades. Carcavelos is fortified with grape spirit during fermentation and, by tradition, sweetened with vinho abafado, must whose fermentation was stopped with spirit, then aged for years in oak until it is amber and nutty. The regional wines and Alenquer reds are made in the international style: destemmed, temperature controlled, aged in French and American oak for the better reds, bottled young for the rest. Óbidos makes sparkling wine by the traditional method.

places.name: Bucelas
places.note: A village in the Trancão valley some 25 kilometres north of Lisbon whose white of Arinto, crisp and long-lived, was famous in Georgian England as Lisbon hock; the DOC is white only and dates from 1911.

places.name: Colares
places.note: The coast beneath the Sintra hills where vines grow own-rooted in dune sand, Ramisco for red and Malvasia for white, sheltered by reed fences; demarcated in 1908 and shrunk by the suburbs to a few hectares, it is one of the few surviving plantings of own-rooted European vines.

places.name: Carcavelos
places.note: The fortified wine of the Estoril coast west of Lisbon, demarcated in 1908, nearly extinct by the 1990s and revived on municipal land at Oeiras.

places.name: Alenquer
places.note: The valley east of the Serra de Montejunto, sheltered from the wind, with the region's best estates and reds from Touriga Nacional, Aragonez, Syrah and Cabernet.

places.name: Serra de Montejunto
places.note: The limestone ridge rising to 666 metres between the coast and Alenquer, the region's rain and wind shield and the reason its reds ripen.

places.name: Torres Vedras and Arruda
places.note: The volume heartland north of Lisbon, co-operative country for decades, now the source of much Vinho Regional Lisboa and of a few serious organic estates.

places.name: Óbidos
places.note: The walled medieval town in the cool north of the region, whose DOC is known for sparkling wine and crisp whites.

places.name: Encostas d'Aire
places.note: The northernmost DOC on the limestone slopes of the Serra de Aire near Leiria, Fátima and Batalha, far from the coast's influence.

places.name: Lourinhã
places.note: A coastal town whose appellation covers grape brandy alone, a rarity it shares with Cognac and Armagnac.

producers.name: Quinta de Chocapalha
producers.why: An Alenquer estate under Montejunto whose Touriga Nacional and Arinto set the modern standard for the region.

producers.name: Quinta do Monte d'Oiro
producers.why: The Alenquer estate that proved Syrah belongs in Lisboa, with Rhône-trained winemaking.

producers.name: Quinta de Pancas
producers.why: A historic Alenquer manor, among the first in Portugal to plant Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay.

producers.name: Casa Santos Lima
producers.why: The large Alenquer house whose varietal regional wines put Lisboa on export shelves everywhere.

producers.name: Adega Regional de Colares
producers.why: The co-operative founded in 1931 that keeps Colares alive, ageing Ramisco in old vats for years before release.

producers.name: Viúva Gomes
producers.why: A Colares house dating from 1808 with a cellar of old vintages that shows how Ramisco ages.

producers.name: Quinta da Romeira
producers.why: The Bucelas estate whose Prova Régia made Arinto a by-the-glass white abroad.

producers.name: Villa Oeiras
producers.why: The municipal estate at Oeiras that brought Carcavelos back from near extinction.

producers.name: Vale da Capucha
producers.why: An organic estate near Torres Vedras that showed the coast's whites could be serious.

terroir.climate: Atlantic and mild, cooler than the latitude suggests: steady westerly wind, sea fog on the coast, mild winters and summers that rarely bake, with rainfall around 600 to 700 millimetres mostly in winter. East of the Montejunto ridge and in the valleys that open towards the Tejo the wind drops and the summers warm, which is where the reds ripen best. The hazards are wind, humidity near the sea and, for the historic DOCs, the city itself.
terroir.soils: Clay and limestone on most of the hills, with Jurassic limestone in the Montejunto ridge and basalt from an old volcanic complex around the city. Colares is the exception: pure dune sand over clay, in which phylloxera cannot live, so its vines are own-rooted. Bucelas sits on limestone and marl in the Trancão valley.
terroir.topography: A country of low coastal hills and valleys running north from Lisbon to Leiria, with the granite massif of Sintra at the coast, the Serra de Montejunto at 666 metres as a spine between Alenquer and the ocean, and the Serra de Aire in the north. Vineyards are mostly below 300 metres on slopes and valley floors; Colares lies almost on the beach.
terroir.water: The Atlantic along the whole western side, and the Tejo estuary to the south-east with the Tejo region beyond it. The Trancão gives Bucelas its valley. The coast's cold water, the Canaries current, is why the sea breeze is cool and why the vines of Colares are grown low against the wind.

traps: Lisboa is the region north of the city; the Setúbal peninsula south of the Tejo is a different region with Castelão and Moscatel.
Bucelas is a white appellation only; Colares makes both colours; Carcavelos is fortified.
Ramisco grows at Colares and nowhere else; it is not a synonym for Castelão.
Lourinhã is a DOC for brandy, not for wine, and the exam likes to ask it.
Aragonez here is Tempranillo, the same grape as Tinta Roriz in the Douro.
Estremadura is the old name of the region; Extremadura is a Spanish region across the border.

wines.note: At least 75 per cent Arinto: pale, bone dry, lemon and green apple over limestone, fine with grilled fish and shellfish; the wine Wellington's officers brought home as Lisbon hock. Some is made sparkling.

Ramisco from the sand dunes: pale garnet, high acid, firm tannin, red fruit turning to earth and sea air, released after years in old wood and aged for decades; a rarity to show a guest, not a wine for the glass.
Malvasia de Colares, waxy, saline and dry, from the same dunes, in tiny quantities.

A fortified, nutty, off-dry to sweet wine from Galego Dourado, Arinto and local grapes, aged in wood, from a handful of hectares between Lisbon and Estoril; a historic curiosity revived by the municipality of Oeiras.
The region's best reds from the shelter of Montejunto: Touriga Nacional, Aragonez, Castelão, Syrah and Cabernet, ripe, polished and oak-aged, good with roast lamb and the grill.
The volume wine in red, white and rosé, international and native grapes side by side, clean, fruity and cheap; the by-the-glass workhorse and the region's export engine.
Traditional method sparkling wine from the cool hills around the walled town, from Arinto, Fernão Pires and Chardonnay.

exam: Say the noble ladder dry to sweet: Sercial, Verdelho, Boal (Bual), Malvasia (Malmsey), with Terrantez as the rarity.
Explain the two ageing routes: estufagem, heated tanks for months, for the young blends; canteiro, cask in a warm loft for years, for the fine wines.
Know Tinta Negra as the red grape that makes most Madeira and may be named on the label since 2015.
Hold the numbers: fortified to seventeen to twenty-two per cent, 85 per cent for a varietal label, Colheita after five years in cask, Frasqueira after twenty.
Give the age ladder: 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50 and over 50 years, each a blend approved by tasting.
Know that sweetness is set by the moment of fortification, early for sweet, late for dry.
Serve it: Sercial and Verdelho cool as aperitifs, Boal and Malmsey with cheese and dessert, and an open bottle keeps for months.

grapes.name: Tinta Negra
grapes.styles: The red grape that makes most of Madeira, hardy and high yielding, vinified at every sweetness level for the three and five year blends and, since 2015, allowed to carry its name on the label; the best lodges show it can be serious.

grapes.name: Sercial
grapes.styles: The dry end of the noble ladder, grown highest and coolest: searing acidity, almond, dried lemon and salt, austere young and long-lived. It is Esgana Cão, dog strangler, on the mainland.

grapes.name: Verdelho
grapes.styles: Medium dry, from the cooler north coast: smoky, nutty, orange peel and a firm acid line, the classic aperitif and soup wine and the grape behind Rainwater's style.

grapes.name: Boal
grapes.styles: Bual in English: medium sweet, from the warm south coast, caramel, raisin, toffee and dried fig with the acidity still cutting; the cheese and dessert wine.

grapes.name: Malvasia
grapes.styles: Malmsey, the sweetest noble style, grown low on the warm south coast: dark toffee, coffee, candied orange and a long tangy finish; Malvasia de São Jorge is the usual planting now, Malvasia Cândida the original.

grapes.name: Terrantez
grapes.styles: A near-extinct noble grape between Verdelho and Boal in sweetness, fragrant and bitter-edged, bottled by only a few lodges and named by examiners for that reason.

grapes.name: Bastardo
grapes.styles: A rare red grape, Trousseau of the Jura, once common and now bottled as a curiosity in medium styles.

law.classification: Madeira is a DOC of fortified wine regulated by IVBAM, the Instituto do Vinho, do Bordado e do Artesanato da Madeira, which tastes, approves and seals every lot. The wine must be fortified to between seventeen and twenty-two per cent from grapes of the island's authorised list, and the categories are set by age, by harvest and by grape rather than by vineyard. The age ladder runs three years, five (Reserve), ten (Special Reserve), fifteen (Extra Reserve), twenty, thirty, forty, fifty and over fifty, each a blend approved as showing the character of that age. Colheita, also sold as Harvest, is a single harvest bottled after at least five years in cask; Frasqueira, also Garrafeira or Vintage, is a single harvest of one grape, nearly always noble, aged at least twenty years in cask by canteiro. A grape on the label means at least 85 per cent of it; since 2015 Tinta Negra may be named like the nobles. Sweetness words, from extra seco to doce, may be used instead of or beside the grape. Rainwater is a defined light medium-dry style. The still wines of the island are a separate DOP, Madeirense, with the regional wine Terras Madeirenses.
labels: The noble grapes, dry to sweet in that order; a grape name means at least 85 per cent.
The English spellings of Boal and Malvasia on export labels.
A rare noble grape, medium, named for its own sake.
The red workhorse, allowed on the label since 2015.
Seco, Meio Seco, Meio Doce, Doce
Dry, medium dry, medium sweet, sweet, with Extra Seco below them: the sweetness words that may replace the grape.
The two ageing routes: heated tank for months, warm loft in cask for years.
Single-vintage Madeira after twenty years in cask; Garrafeira and Vintage are its other names.
Single-harvest Madeira after five years in cask.
The island's unfortified table wines: a separate DOP and its regional wine.
tiers: Madeira, three years
The youngest wine, often Finest or a sweetness word alone, usually Tinta Negra by estufagem; it may wear no age at all.
Reserve, five years; Special Reserve, ten; Extra Reserve, fifteen
Age-stated blends, mostly canteiro from ten years upward, approved by tasting as showing the character of that age.
20, 30, 40, 50 and over 50 years
The older age statements, blends of canteiro wine of at least that character; the oldest categories were opened in recent decades.
Colheita (Harvest)
One harvest, bottled after at least five years in cask; any grape, Tinta Negra included.
Frasqueira (Garrafeira, Vintage)
One harvest and a single grape, nearly always a noble one, at least twenty years in cask by canteiro; the top of the island.
Rainwater
A light, pale, medium-dry style, a legal category of its own.
Solera
A dated, refreshed blend; the year is when the solera was laid down, not a vintage, and the category is now rare and tightly ruled.

made.viticulture: Madeira's vineyards are terraces, poios, held by dry-stone walls on slopes that are often too steep for anything but a hoe, and they are tiny: the island is a place of smallholders who sell to the lodges, and a vineyard is a few rows beside a house, bananas and vegetables. The vine is trained on low pergolas, latadas, that lift the fruit into the breeze above the humidity, with the ground beneath sometimes cropped; wire training on the few flatter sites is recent. Rain, mildew and rot are the hazards, far more than drought, and the growers spray and pick early: the island wants acidity, not sugar, since the fortification will set the sweetness, and the grapes come in at modest ripeness through August and September, the lower warm south coast first and the high Sercial plots last. The noble grapes are a small minority of the plantings and are grown where they do best, Sercial and Verdelho high and on the north coast, Boal and Malvasia low on the sunny south coast around Câmara de Lobos and Calheta; Tinta Negra is everywhere. Oidium in 1852 and phylloxera in 1872 wrecked the old vineyard and brought in hybrid direct producers, which may not go into Madeira wine, and the replanting that followed is why Tinta Negra dominates. Porto Santo, the sandy sister island, grows a little on its own ground.
made.winemaking: The must ferments, with or without skins, and is fortified with neutral grape spirit to seventeen to eighteen per cent; a sweet style is stopped early with most of its sugar unfermented, a dry one is allowed to ferment almost out first, so the grape and the moment of fortification set the sweetness together. Estufagem warms the wine in tanks at around forty-five to fifty degrees for at least three months: the method for the three-year and most five-year blends, mostly Tinta Negra, invented in the 1790s to copy the sea voyage, the vinho da roda, that had improved casks sent as ballast to the Indies. Canteiro ages the wine in old casks on racks under the lodge roof, where the sun warms it slowly over years: the method for the noble grapes, the age-stated blends from ten years upwards, Colheita and Frasqueira, and the wine loses volume to evaporation and gains concentration, rancio and tang. Both routes give a wine already oxidised and stable, so an open bottle lasts months and a sealed one a century. Blends are assembled for an age statement and approved by tasting; Colheita is one harvest bottled after five years in cask; Frasqueira is one harvest of a single grape, nearly always noble, after twenty years in cask; a solera, dated to the year it was laid down, is a refreshed blend whose date is not a vintage. A varietal label needs 85 per cent of the grape, and the regulator seals every bottle.

places.name: Funchal
places.note: The capital and port on the south coast where the lodges stand and the wine is aged, blended and shipped; the city's lofts are where canteiro happens, and the oldest stocks on the island lie in its cellars.

places.name: Câmara de Lobos
places.note: The fishing town west of Funchal and the heart of the south coast vineyard, warm and sunny: the home of Tinta Negra, Boal and Malvasia and of two of the island's producing houses, with the terraces of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos climbing behind it and, to the west under a cliff, the Fajã dos Padres with its old Malvasia Cândida vines, reached by cable car.

places.name: Estreito de Câmara de Lobos
places.note: The parish above the town, the island's most important vine parish, where the terraces rise through the warm belt of Tinta Negra into Boal and, higher, Sercial and Verdelho.

places.name: Jardim da Serra
places.note: The high parish above Estreito, cool and often in cloud, where Sercial grows at the top of its range.

places.name: Calheta
places.note: The sunny south-western coast beyond Câmara de Lobos, warm enough for Malvasia and Boal low by the sea, with terraces of Tinta Negra above them.

places.name: São Vicente and the north coast
places.note: Wetter, cloudier and cooler, facing the trade winds: the north-coast parishes of São Vicente, Seixal and Porto Moniz grow Verdelho and Sercial on narrow ledges above the sea, and much Tinta Negra on the lower slopes.

places.name: Porto Santo
places.note: The flat, sandy sister island to the north-east, dry and hot, with a little wine of its own on sand and limestone, traditionally from the white Caracol and Listrão; its grapes may go into Madeira.

producers.name: Blandy's
producers.why: Founded in 1811 and the best known of the British names of the Madeira Wine Company, with the reference Frasqueiras and the Funchal lodge where canteiro can be seen.

producers.name: Henriques and Henriques
producers.why: A Câmara de Lobos house of 1850 with vineyards of its own, a dry-leaning style built on Sercial and Verdelho, and a reliable Terrantez.

producers.name: Barbeito
producers.why: The house, founded in 1946, that stopped adding caramel and showed what single-cask and unblended Tinta Negra could be.

producers.name: Broadbent
producers.why: An importer's label rather than a lodge: single-cask Madeiras selected for the North American market across the grape ladder.

producers.name: Cossart Gordon
producers.why: Founded in 1745, the oldest shipping name on the island, a brand of the Madeira Wine Company since the 1950s, known for a drier house style.

producers.name: Justino's
producers.why: Founded in 1870 and one of the island's largest producers, from three-year blends to very old Frasqueiras.

producers.name: Pereira d'Oliveira
producers.why: A family house of 1850 in Funchal famous for selling Frasqueiras from the nineteenth century directly from its lodge.

producers.name: Madeira Wine Company
producers.why: The group formed from the Madeira Wine Association of 1913 that gathered Blandy's, Cossart Gordon, Leacock's and Miles, most of the historic British names.
