terroir.climate: Subtropical and maritime, warm all year with little frost, humid, and wet on the north coast where the trade winds drop their rain; the south coast around Funchal is drier and sunnier. Heat and humidity bring mildew and rot, so the vines are lifted off the ground and the grapes are picked early and acid. The climate that makes the vineyard difficult is the same one that ages the wine in the lofts.
terroir.soils: Volcanic: red and brown clay weathered from basalt, rich in iron and potassium, acid, held on the slopes by dry-stone walls. It is fertile enough to need no feeding and drains well, but there is little depth of it, and on Porto Santo the soil is sand and limestone instead.
terroir.topography: A steep island rising to Pico Ruivo at 1,862 metres within a few kilometres of the sea, so that almost every vineyard is a terrace, a poio, cut into a hillside or a cliff. Vines grow from sea level to about eight hundred metres, the noble grapes higher and cooler, Tinta Negra lower and on the north coast's wetter ledges.
terroir.water: The Atlantic on every side, moderating the heat and bringing the humidity; the levadas, the stone irrigation channels that carry water from the wet north across the mountains to the dry south, are what made the terraces farmable. Casks once crossed that ocean to the Indies and came home better, and the lodges learned to copy the voyage with heat.

traps: Boal and Bual are one grape; Malvasia and Malmsey are one grape and one style. The ladder runs Sercial, Verdelho, Boal, Malvasia, driest to sweetest.
Frasqueira and Colheita are both single-harvest Madeiras, but Frasqueira needs twenty years in cask and a single grape, nearly always a noble one; Colheita five years and any grape.
A solera date is the year the solera was laid down, never a vintage.
Rainwater is a style, light and medium dry, not a grape and not a region.
Tinta Negra is red, and most Madeira is made from it; the noble grapes are a small minority of the vineyard.
Estufagem is the fast route in a heated tank; canteiro is the slow route in cask under the roof. Both cook the wine on purpose, and neither is a solera.
Madeira wine is fortified; the island's table wines are a separate appellation, Madeirense.
Sercial is grown high and cool, Malvasia low and warm: the sweet grape takes the sunniest ground.

wines.note: Pale amber, dry, piercing acidity, almonds and dried citrus; serve cool as an aperitif with olives, salted almonds, consommé or smoked fish. The blind-tasting shock: fortified and bone dry.
Medium dry, golden, smoky and nutty with orange peel; cool, with soups, pâté, mushroom dishes and hard cheese.
Medium sweet, amber to brown, toffee and raisin with a tang of acid; cellar cool with cheese, caramel desserts, nut tarts and bread pudding.
Sweet and dark, coffee, dark toffee and candied orange, cut by acidity so it never cloys; with chocolate, pecan pie, blue cheese or alone after dinner.
A light, pale, medium-dry blend, usually Tinta Negra, named for the casks said to have been diluted by rain on the quay; the American market's Madeira, served cool as an aperitif or in cooking.

One harvest, a single grape, nearly always one of the nobles, at least twenty years in cask by canteiro before bottling: the summit of the island, intense, layered and apparently immortal, poured in small measures.

exam: The three floors: DOC, Vinho Regional, Vinho, and which word is Portugal's IGP.
Reserva against Garrafeira: one is ripeness, the other is time, and only Garrafeira demands months in bottle.
The two names of Tempranillo, Tinta Roriz in the north and Aragonez in the south.
Port's two families, Ruby and Tawny, with Vintage, LBV and Colheita placed correctly.
Madeira's four noble grapes from dry to sweet: Sercial, Verdelho, Bual, Malmsey.
The home of each signature grape: Baga, Encruzado, Alvarinho, Castelão, Alicante Bouschet.
The dates that anchor the story: 1703, 1756, 1908, 1986.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.styles: The national red: perfumed with violets and bergamot, deep in colour, firm in tannin, the backbone of Port and of dry Douro and Dão reds, now planted in every region.

grapes.name: Touriga Franca
grapes.styles: The Douro's most planted grape, late ripening, floral and softer than its namesake, the flesh of a Port blend.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: Tinta Roriz in the Douro and the Dão, Aragonez in the Alentejo and Lisboa: one grape under two Portuguese names, bringing fruit and body to blends.

grapes.name: Baga
grapes.styles: Bairrada's grape: small berries, high acid and tannin, cherry and tobacco, ageing for decades and the base of its sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Castelão
grapes.styles: The sandy south's red, also called Periquita: raspberry and leather, the grape of the Setúbal peninsula, the Tejo and Lisboa.

grapes.name: Trincadeira
grapes.styles: Tinta Amarela in the Douro: spicy, rot-prone, at home in the dry Alentejo.

grapes.name: Alicante Bouschet
grapes.styles: A teinturier with red flesh and red juice, French by birth and Portuguese by adoption in the Alentejo, where it gives colour and depth.

grapes.name: Alfrocheiro
grapes.styles: A deep-coloured, soft red of the Dão and Bairrada, valued in blends for fruit and balance.

grapes.name: Mencía
grapes.styles: Jaen in the Dão: Galicia's fragrant red across the border, early ripening and lighter in tannin.

grapes.name: Alvarinho
grapes.styles: The Albariño of Galicia under its Portuguese name: the fuller, more serious white of Vinho Verde, at its best in Monção e Melgaço.

grapes.name: Loureiro
grapes.styles: Vinho Verde's floral, laurel-scented white, the grape of the Lima valley.

grapes.name: Arinto
grapes.styles: The acid keeper: crisp, citrus whites that hold their nerve in the heat, the grape of Bucelas, called Pedernã in Vinho Verde.

grapes.name: Encruzado
grapes.styles: The Dão's noble white: textured, mineral, takes oak and age like a white Burgundy.

grapes.name: Fernão Pires
grapes.styles: Portugal's most planted white, Maria Gomes in Bairrada: aromatic, soft, the base of much Tejo and Lisboa white and of sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Antão Vaz
grapes.styles: The Alentejo's white, heat tolerant and full, from Vidigueira.

grapes.name: Muscat
grapes.styles: Moscatel de Setúbal, the Muscat of Alexandria, makes the fortified wine of the Setúbal peninsula; Moscatel Galego, the small-berried Muscat, makes Moscatel do Douro at Favaios.

grapes.name: Tinta Negra
grapes.styles: Madeira's workhorse red grape, the base of most blended and age-indicated Madeira.

labels: Not an ageing word: a stated vintage and at least half a degree of alcohol above the regional minimum, so it promises ripeness and selection.

The ageing word: a red matured at least thirty months with twelve in bottle, a white at least twelve months with six in bottle, plus the Reserva alcohol margin. In Port it is a rare style of Niepoort's, cask then large glass demijohns.
A selected harvest: a vintage-dated wine held to a higher alcohol floor than the ordinary wine, close to Reserva in meaning.
The harvest, so the vintage on a still wine; on a Port label it names the single-harvest tawny.
Estate: quinta in the north, herdade for the big farms of the Alentejo, casa and paço for a manor house.
Grape variety; castas is the plural on a back label.
Fortified wine: Port, Madeira, Moscatel de Setúbal, Carcavelos.
Bottled at the estate; engarrafado por names the bottler.
Old vines, often a mixed field blend in the Douro or the Dão.
Literally mature: the old word for any still wine that is not Vinho Verde.
A winery or cellar; Adega Cooperativa is a co-operative.
ladder: Denominação de Origem Controlada, the European DOP: the top tier, a demarcated region with its own grape list, yields and tasting approval, run by a regional commission (CVR), or for Port and Madeira by the IVDP and IVBAM.

The regional wine tier: fourteen broad areas, among them Minho, Duriense, Terras do Dão, Beira Atlântico, Lisboa, Tejo, Península de Setúbal, Alentejano and Algarve, with wider grape lists and room for international varieties.
Wine with no geographical claim, the old vinho de mesa; it may name a grape and a vintage under the European rules.
portugal.overview:
Portugal's wine story begins with the sea. The country is long and thin, with the ocean down the whole of its western side, and the mountains that run parallel to the coast decide which places are wet and green and which are hot and dry. The Minho in the north-west takes the Atlantic full on and is among the wettest wine regions in Europe; the Serra do Marão stops that weather, and the Douro behind it is a sun trap of schist terraces. The Caramulo and the Serra da Estrela ring the granite of the Dão. South of the Tejo the land flattens into the Alentejo's cork oak plains, where summer is rainless. The islands are separate worlds: Madeira a volcanic rock in the subtropical Atlantic, the Azores further out still.

The trade shaped the north. Port was born of England's wars with France: the Methuen Treaty of 1703 gave Portuguese wine a tariff advantage, the shippers of Porto built an industry on the Douro's wine, and in 1756 the Marquis of Pombal demarcated the valley and put its trade under a chartered company, which makes the Douro one of the first regulated wine regions in the world. A second wave of demarcation in 1907 and 1908 named Vinho Verde, Dão, Colares, Carcavelos, Setúbal and Madeira. Then came decades of stagnation, co-operatives and bulk, until Portugal joined the European Community in 1986 and its DOC system, its regional wines and a new generation of estates took shape.

The law has three floors. DOC, Denominação de Origem Controlada, the European DOP, is the top: around thirty of them, each with a regional commission, a list of grapes and a tasting panel. Vinho Regional is the IGP, fourteen broad areas such as Minho, Duriense, Terras do Dão, Beira Atlântico, Lisboa, Tejo, Península de Setúbal and Alentejano, with a longer list of grapes and looser rules, and plain Vinho sits below. Alongside the origin words run the quality words: Reserva asks for a stated vintage and half a degree of alcohol above the regional minimum; Colheita Seleccionada is a vintage selection with its own higher alcohol floor; Garrafeira alone is an ageing term, thirty months for a red of which twelve are in bottle, twelve months for a white of which six are in bottle.

The exam leans on the Douro and on Port above everything else, then on Vinho Verde's style and the Alvarinho of Monção e Melgaço, on Madeira's four noble grapes in order of sweetness, and on the signatures of the Dão, Bairrada and the Alentejo. Learn the grapes by their homes: Touriga Nacional everywhere, Baga in Bairrada, Encruzado in the Dão, Castelão on sand in the south, Alicante Bouschet with its red flesh in the Alentejo, Arinto for acid that survives heat, and the double name of Tempranillo. Portugal also grows around half of the world's cork, most of it in the Alentejo, which is why a cork question so often has a Portuguese answer.

traps: Vinho Verde means young wine, not green wine, and it can be red, rosé or sparkling as well as white.
Reserva in Portugal is not a time word; Garrafeira is, and it is nothing like the Spanish Gran Reserva in its minimums.
Colheita on a Port is a tawny from one harvest, aged in wood; a Vintage Port is a ruby from one harvest, aged in bottle.
A tawny's 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 Years is an indication of the blend's average age, never a vintage.
Moscatel de Setúbal is Muscat of Alexandria; the Douro's Moscatel Galego is the small-berried Muscat.
Alicante Bouschet is a French teinturier, not a Portuguese native, however much the Alentejo has adopted it.
The Douro is a river and a region in Portugal; the same river is the Duero in Spain, where Ribera del Duero grows Tempranillo.

exam: Place the peninsula south of Lisbon between the Tagus and Sado estuaries, with the Arrábida on its south coast and the Palmela sand inland.
Define Moscatel de Setúbal: Muscat of Alexandria, fortified during fermentation, macerated on its skins after fortification, aged oxidatively in wood.
Know the two DOCs and the regional wine: Setúbal for the fortified Muscat, Palmela for Castelão table wine, Península de Setúbal (Terras do Sado until 2009) around them.
Give Castelão as the red grape of the sand and Periquita as the brand name that became its nickname.
Separate the two Fonsecas: José Maria da Fonseca of Azeitão and Fonseca the Port shipper of Gaia.
At the Advanced level hold the percentages, 85 for the traditional names and 67 for plain Setúbal, and Moscatel Roxo.

grapes.name: Moscatel de Setúbal
grapes.styles: Muscat of Alexandria under its local name: big-berried, high in sugar, grapey and orange-scented, grown on the Arrábida's limestone for the fortified wine that carries the region's name.

grapes.name: Moscatel Roxo
grapes.styles: A pink-skinned Muscat, rare and prized, which makes a more perfumed, rose-tinged fortified wine labelled Moscatel Roxo de Setúbal.

grapes.name: Castelão
grapes.styles: The peninsula's red, at home on Palmela's sand: raspberry, dried herb and tobacco, firm in youth and gentle after a decade; the grape behind the Periquita brand since 1850.

grapes.name: Fernão Pires
grapes.styles: The aromatic white of the plain, soft and floral, drunk young or blended with Arinto in the regional whites.

grapes.name: Arinto
grapes.styles: The acid in the white blends, lemony and firm, and the grape of the few serious dry whites of the peninsula.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Ripe, dark and peppery on the sand, a mainstay of the regional reds and of many Castelão blends.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Planted in the Arrábida foothills from the 1970s for a Bordeaux-styled estate red that put the peninsula's table wine on the map.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.styles: Perfume and colour in the regional blends, usually beside Castelão and Syrah.

law.classification: The peninsula holds two DOCs and a regional wine. DOC Setúbal is the fortified Muscat: a wine labelled Moscatel de Setúbal or Moscatel Roxo de Setúbal must take at least 85 per cent of its must from that grape, and a wine with at least 67 per cent Moscatel may be labelled plainly Setúbal, under the statute of the denomination. The DOC admits age indications on the aged blends and the terms Colheita and Superior. DOC Palmela, demarcated on the sandy plain, is for table wine and requires its reds to be at least two thirds Castelão; whites and rosés are also allowed. Vinho Regional Península de Setúbal covers the whole peninsula with a wider grape list, and it was called Terras do Sado until the renaming of 2009. The Comissão Vitivinícola Regional da Península de Setúbal certifies all three.
labels: Fortified Muscat of Alexandria from the DOC, at least 85 per cent of the grape.
The pink-skinned Muscat, labelled Moscatel Roxo de Setúbal.
On its own: the fortified wine with 67 to 85 per cent Moscatel.
A selected lot of Moscatel of higher quality, held longer before release.
An age indication on an aged Moscatel blend; the number describes the blend, not one harvest.
A Moscatel from a single harvest, vintage dated.
A brand name of the oldest house that became a popular synonym for Castelão; the grape's name on a label is Castelão.
The regional wine's name until 2009, still on older bottles.
tiers: DOC Setúbal
The fortified Muscat: Moscatel de Setúbal or Moscatel Roxo de Setúbal needs at least 85 per cent of that grape; plain Setúbal at least 67 per cent.
DOC Palmela
Table wine from the sandy plain; a red must be at least two thirds Castelão.
Vinho Regional Península de Setúbal
The regional wine over the whole peninsula, Terras do Sado until 2009; it takes Syrah, Cabernet, Touriga Nacional and the rest.
Vinho
Wine with no origin claim.

made.viticulture: The Moscatel grows where the Arrábida's limestone gives way to clay around Azeitão, on low vines in rows; Muscat of Alexandria needs the heat of that south-facing wall of rock to reach the sugar the fortified wine wants, and it is picked late, in September, at high ripeness. Moscatel Roxo is planted in small, treasured parcels. On the Palmela plain Castelão is grown on sand, bush trained in the old vineyards and on wire in the new, the roots going deep for water; the sand drains so fast that vigour is low and the grape ripens small and even, and because phylloxera moves poorly through pure sand some old plots stand on their own roots. Irrigation is allowed and used on the plain. The hazards are different in the two zones: on the Arrábida, drought and the sea wind; on the sand, heat spikes that cook the fruit and the autumn humidity off the two estuaries that brings rot to thin-skinned grapes. Harvest begins in August for the whites and the Syrah and runs to late September for Castelão and the Moscatel. The international reds planted since the 1970s, Cabernet first and Syrah after, sit in the foothills and on the plain's edge.
made.winemaking: Moscatel de Setúbal is made the way the French make a vin doux naturel, with one step of its own. The must ferments on its skins for a few days, then grape spirit is added before the sugar is gone, stopping the yeast and leaving the wine sweet at around seventeen to eighteen per cent alcohol. The skins are then returned, or left, in the fortified wine for months through the winter, and that maceration after fortification is what gives the wine its deep orange-peel aroma and its grip; few other Muscats are made this way. The wine is racked off the skins in spring and goes to old wood, where it ages oxidatively: a few years for the basic bottling, five, ten, twenty, thirty or forty years for the aged wines sold with an age indication, and a lifetime for the oldest casks that the lodges still hold. A Colheita is one harvest; Superior marks a selected lot. The red table wines of Palmela are made in the modern Portuguese way, destemmed, fermented in stainless steel or concrete, aged in French and American oak for the Reserva; Castelão takes well to old wood and to a few years in bottle. The regional whites are cold fermented and bottled young.

places.name: Serra da Arrábida
places.note: The limestone ridge along the south coast, rising to about five hundred metres and falling to the sea in cliffs: its clay and limestone flanks grow the Moscatel de Setúbal and the peninsula's Cabernet, and its slopes are a natural park, so the vineyards stop at the trees.

places.name: Azeitão
places.note: The village at the foot of the Arrábida where the region's two historic houses have their lodges and cellars: the home of Moscatel de Setúbal, of the Periquita brand and of the peninsula's first Cabernet, with a sheep's cheese and a sweet pastry of its own.

places.name: Palmela
places.note: The castle town and the DOC of the sandy plain north and east of it: Castelão on deep, poor sand, some of it ungrafted, making the firm raspberry-and-tobacco reds that soften over ten years. The co-operative at Pegões and the family estates of Fernando Pó are its working heart.

places.name: Pegões
places.note: The village on the plain whose co-operative, founded in the 1950s on a government settlement scheme, became the peninsula's most reliable source of inexpensive Castelão, Syrah and Fernão Pires.

places.name: Setúbal
places.note: The port city on the Sado estuary, a harbour of fishing and shipping, which gave the fortified wine its name and shipped it; the vineyards lie west of it under the Arrábida.

places.name: Sado estuary
places.note: The river mouth south of the peninsula, salt marsh, rice and dolphins, which named the regional wine until 2009 and sends the morning humidity over the Palmela sand.

producers.name: José Maria da Fonseca
producers.why: The Azeitão house founded in 1834 that made Moscatel de Setúbal a category, created Periquita in 1850 and holds the oldest casks on the peninsula; it is not the Port house.

producers.name: Bacalhôa Vinhos de Portugal
producers.why: The Azeitão company, formerly J.P. Vinhos, whose Quinta da Bacalhôa Cabernet of the 1970s and aged Moscatels made it the region's other reference.

producers.name: Adega de Pegões
producers.why: The co-operative of the Palmela plain, the dependable source of the peninsula's everyday Castelão, Syrah and Fernão Pires at every price.

producers.name: Casa Ermelinda Freitas
producers.why: A family estate at Fernando Pó on the Palmela sand that built its name on Castelão and old-vine reds under the DOC Palmela and the regional label.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean with the Atlantic close: warm, dry summers and mild, wet winters, the sea breeze crossing the peninsula every afternoon. The Arrábida's south-facing slopes above the water are the warmest and ripen Moscatel to high sugar; the sandy plain of Palmela is hot by day and cool at night; the northern shore facing the Tagus is the coolest ground.
terroir.soils: Two soils, one wine each. The Serra da Arrábida is limestone and clay, pale and stony, and it gives the Moscatel its ripeness and its grip. The Palmela plain is deep, poor sand over clay, warm and free draining, where Castelão roots deep and ripens evenly; phylloxera travels badly through it, so some old vines remain on their own roots.
terroir.topography: A broad peninsula pointing south-west, flat and low across most of its width, with the Arrábida rising abruptly to about five hundred metres along the south coast and dropping to the sea in cliffs. The best Moscatel grows on its north and south flanks around Azeitão; the Castelão country is the sandy plain north and east of Palmela's castle hill.
terroir.water: The Tagus to the north and the Sado to the south are both estuaries, and between them the peninsula is never far from salt water. The Sado gave the old regional name, Terras do Sado, and its mouth at Setúbal is the port the Moscatel sailed from.

traps: Moscatel de Setúbal is Muscat of Alexandria, the big-berried Muscat; the Douro's Moscatel Galego, Beaumes-de-Venise and Frontignan are the small-berried Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains.
Setúbal DOC is a fortified wine only; the peninsula's table wines are Palmela DOC or Vinho Regional Península de Setúbal.
Periquita is a brand, not a grape: the grape is Castelão, and the brand belongs to one house.
José Maria da Fonseca is a Setúbal table and Moscatel house; Fonseca is a Port house. Two different families, two different wines.
The skins are returned after fortification, not before; that is what sets this Muscat apart from a vin doux naturel.
An age indication on a Moscatel (10, 20, 30, 40 Anos) describes a blend; Colheita names one harvest.
Terras do Sado on an older label is the same regional wine as Península de Setúbal.

wines.note: Amber to gold, around seventeen to eighteen per cent, sweet and grapey when young with orange peel and honey, darkening to toffee, dried fig and bitter marmalade with decades in wood; the acidity keeps it lively. Serve cool in a small glass with almond tart, orange desserts, crème caramel or blue cheese, or on its own after dinner.
The rare pink Muscat: rosier, spicier and more floral than the white, usually released older and poured as a rarity by the glass.

Castelão-led red from the sand, raspberry and tobacco, medium-bodied with a firm, dry finish, softened by a year in oak in the Reserva; the classic pairing is roast kid, grilled sardines or a plate of cured ham.
Blends of Castelão, Syrah, Touriga Nacional, Aragonez and Cabernet: ripe, dark, easy reds at a kind price, served slightly cool with grilled meats.
wines.style: Vinho Regional Península de Setúbal tinto

wines.note: Fernão Pires and Arinto, sometimes Chardonnay or Verdelho: soft, aromatic, cold, for the fried fish and shellfish of the Sado coast.

exam: Place the Tejo on the Tagus north-east of Lisbon, inland from Lisboa and north of the Alentejo, and know it was the Ribatejo until 2009.
Name the three zones, Bairro, Campo and Charneca, and say which is clay hills, which floodplain and which sand.
Give the lead grapes: Fernão Pires and Arinto for white, Castelão, Trincadeira and Touriga Nacional for red.
Know that most Tejo wine is sold as Vinho Regional Tejo, the tier with the longer grape list and the looser rules.
Hold the synonyms: Fernão Pires is Maria Gomes in Bairrada, Castelão was sold as Periquita, Trincadeira is Tinta Amarela.

grapes.name: Fernão Pires
grapes.styles: The region's white workhorse, aromatic and soft, grapey and floral, best drunk young and often blended with Arinto for acidity; Bairrada calls the same grape Maria Gomes.

grapes.name: Castelão
grapes.styles: The red of the sandy south bank, medium-bodied, raspberry and dried herb, firm when young and leathery with age; the grape sold for decades as Periquita.

grapes.name: Trincadeira
grapes.styles: Spicy, peppery and dark fruited when it ripens cleanly, and prone to rot in a damp autumn; the lift in many traditional blends. It is Tinta Amarela in the north.

grapes.name: Touriga Nacional
grapes.styles: Planted widely since the 1990s for perfume, colour and structure in the ambitious reds of the Bairro and the Charneca.

grapes.name: Arinto
grapes.styles: The acid-keeping white blended with Fernão Pires; on its own it is lean, lemony and able to take a little oak.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The international red that has taken best to the Tejo's heat, giving ripe, dark, peppery wines under the Vinho Regional label.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Grown for blends with Touriga Nacional and for varietal bottlings; it ripens fully in the Charneca's sand.

grapes.name: Tempranillo
grapes.styles: As Tinta Roriz or Aragonez, a filler of colour and body in reds that lead with Touriga or Castelão.

law.classification: The DOC Ribatejo took its statute by decree in 2000, with the regional wine around it as Vinho Regional Ribatejano. In 2009 both were renamed after the river, DOC do Tejo and Vinho Regional Tejo, so that the labels and the region's name agreed and the old name's association with bulk wine was shed. The DOC carries six sub-regions that may be named on the label: Almeirim, Cartaxo, Chamusca, Coruche, Santarém and Tomar. The DOC's grape lists are drawn sub-region by sub-region and rest on Fernão Pires, Arinto, Castelão, Trincadeira and Touriga Nacional, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot admitted in the statute of 2000; the Vinho Regional, under the Comissão Vitivinícola Regional do Tejo, carries a longer list still, Syrah, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc among them, and looser rules. The three zones, Bairro, Campo and Charneca, are the growers' and the trade's words for the terroir, not legal names on a label. Reserva and Garrafeira follow the national rules.
labels: The region's name until 2009; it means the banks of the Tagus and still appears on older bottles.
The northern hills of clay and limestone, the zone of the firmer reds.
The sandy, dry south bank, warm and poor, where Castelão and the international reds ripen.
The alluvial floodplain of the river, fertile and high yielding.
A vintage-dated wine of at least half a degree more alcohol than the regional minimum, often oaked.
A selected harvest, vintage dated, held to its own alcohol floor above the regional minimum.
Estate names; the Tejo's great farms are quintas and casais.
tiers: DOC do Tejo
The appellation of the Tagus valley, called DOC Ribatejo until 2009: its own grape lists, drawn sub-region by sub-region, and six sub-regions that may be named.
DOC do Tejo with a sub-region
Almeirim, Cartaxo, Chamusca, Coruche, Santarém or Tomar on the label: the wine comes from that sub-region alone.
Vinho Regional Tejo
The regional wine, formerly Ribatejano, over the same land: a longer grape list, looser rules, and the tier most Tejo wine wears.
Vinho
Wine with no origin claim, the old vinho de mesa; the floodplain's bulk wine lived here.

made.viticulture: The Tejo was planted for volume: the Lezíria's deep silt makes vines grow like weeds, and through the twentieth century the floodplain and its co-operatives filled bulk wine for Lisbon and the colonies. Since the 1990s the better growers have moved the vine off the plain, where the state has paid to pull vineyards and plant other crops, and onto the clay-limestone hills of the Bairro and the sand of the Charneca, which stress the vine, cut the yield and ripen a smaller, darker grape. Training is on wires with spur or cane pruning, rows wide enough for machines on the flat and tighter on the slopes. Irrigation is allowed and common on the sand, where the summer is dry and the soil holds nothing. Harvest runs from mid August for the whites into late September for Touriga and Cabernet, by machine on the big estates and by hand on the old mixed plots. The hazards are rot in Trincadeira after an autumn rain, sunburn on the south bank and the loss of acidity in a hot year, which is why Arinto stays in every white blend. The fruit shares the land with horses, fighting bulls, cork oak, olives and rice: the Ribatejo was always a farm before it was a vineyard.
made.winemaking: The whites are made cold and fast: night picking or early morning, gentle pressing, settling, a cool fermentation in stainless steel and bottling within months, so that Fernão Pires keeps the floral lift that it loses with age. A few estates ferment Arinto or Chardonnay in barrel and leave it on the lees for weight. The reds are destemmed, fermented in steel or in concrete at moderate temperatures with pumping over, and the serious ones go to French or American oak for a year, with Reserva and Garrafeira carrying the national rules on alcohol and time. The Tejo's style is ripe and rounded rather than tannic, and winemakers blend for it: Touriga Nacional for perfume and colour, Castelão for freshness and tannin, Trincadeira for spice, Syrah or Cabernet for flesh. The regional tier, Vinho Regional Tejo, carries the longer grape list and the looser rules, which is why most labels wear it; the DOC's lists are narrower and drawn sub-region by sub-region, though they admit Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot beside the Portuguese grapes. Traditional method sparkling and a little sweet or late harvest wine are made but seldom leave the region.

places.name: Bairro
places.note: The north bank's hills of clay, limestone and some schist, running from Santarém up to Tomar: cooler, wetter and later than the plain, the source of the Tejo's most structured reds and of its firmest Arinto.

places.name: Tomar
places.note: The northernmost sub-region, around the Templar town on the Nabão: the coolest and hilliest corner of the Tejo, with limestone and schist and fresher whites.

places.name: Santarém
places.note: The regional capital above the river, with the Bairro's slopes behind it; its name is one of the six sub-regions of the DOC.

places.name: Cartaxo
places.note: A sub-region on the north bank below Santarém, part hill and part plain, long a centre of co-operative production and now of estate reds.

places.name: Campo
places.note: The Lezíria, the floodplain of the Tagus: deep, fertile silt that floods in winter and gives huge crops of soft wine. It carried the region's bulk trade and is now largely given to other crops, with vines kept where the levees hold the soil drier.

places.name: Almeirim
places.note: The sub-region on the south bank opposite Santarém, where the plain meets the sand and the Tejo's oldest estates stand; the fullest reds of the DOC come from its edge.

places.name: Chamusca
places.note: A riverside sub-region upstream of Almeirim on the plain, with cork oak and rice beside the vines.

places.name: Charneca
places.note: The south bank's dry plain of sand, pine, cork oak and heath: poor, hot and well drained, it ripens Castelão, Syrah and Cabernet to a dark, soft wine. Irrigation is usual here.

places.name: Coruche
places.note: The southernmost sub-region, on the Sorraia river in the sand of the Charneca, next to the cork oak country of the Alentejo.

producers.name: Quinta da Alorna
producers.why: An Almeirim estate dating from 1723, named for a marquisate won in India, and one of the Tejo's oldest names for estate reds and Fernão Pires.

producers.name: Casal Branco
producers.why: An old family estate at Almeirim whose falconry label carries the Tejo's firmer traditional-grape reds and oak-aged whites.

producers.name: Quinta da Lagoalva de Cima
producers.why: A large estate at Alpiarça on the south bank that grows Touriga Nacional and Syrah beside horses and cork, the modern Tejo on one farm.

producers.name: Companhia das Lezírias
producers.why: The great farm company of the floodplain, founded in 1836, which shows what the Campo and the Charneca sand can do when yields are held down.

terroir.climate: Warm and dry in summer with a Mediterranean pattern of winter rain, but the Tagus estuary lets Atlantic air up the valley, so the river plain is milder and more humid than the plains to the east. The south bank is the hottest and driest ground; the northern hills towards Tomar are cooler and wetter. Frost is rare and ripeness is seldom the problem; keeping acidity is.
terroir.soils: Three soils, one per zone: deep alluvial silt and clay on the floodplain, fertile enough to make vines vigorous; poor sand with some gravel on the south bank, the Charneca; and clay with limestone, some schist and sandstone in the northern hills, the Bairro. The hills and the sand give the better wines, the plain the bigger yields.
terroir.topography: A broad, low river valley running south-west towards Lisbon. The Lezíria, the floodplain of the Tagus, is almost flat and floods in a wet winter. North of the river the land rises into rolling hills and small ridges; south of it the Charneca is a low, dry plain of sand, pine and cork oak.
terroir.water: The Tejo, the Tagus, is the whole point: it floods the Campo, carries sea air inland and divides the clay north bank from the sandy south bank. The Zêzere, which joins it from the north, and the Nabão, which runs through Tomar, cut the northern hills.

traps: The Tejo is a river region and a wine region; Lisboa is the coastal region beside it, and both were renamed in the same years (Lisboa was Estremadura).
Bairro is a zone of the Tejo; Bairrada is a separate DOC far to the north on clay by the Atlantic.
The Tejo's sand is the Charneca on the south bank; the clay is on the north bank, the opposite of what a reader guesses from the Alentejo.
Tinta Roriz and Aragonez are both Tempranillo, and the Tejo uses both names.
Vinho Regional Tejo is not a lesser wine in quality terms: the estates choose it for its freedom in grapes and blending.

wines.note: Fernão Pires with Arinto, sometimes Sauvignon Blanc or Chardonnay: aromatic, soft, orange blossom and pear, drunk cold and young with grilled fish, clams and salads. The glass pour of the region.

A blend led by Castelão, Trincadeira and Touriga Nacional from the Bairro or the Charneca: medium to full, ripe red and black fruit, dried herb, moderate tannin, a year or two of oak in the Reserva. It takes roast pork, duck and grilled lamb.
Where most of the Syrah and the international blends go: ripe, plush, generous reds at a kind price, the Tejo's calling card abroad. Serve a touch cool with burgers, barbecue and spiced dishes.
Castelão or Touriga Nacional pressed pink: strawberry, dry and light, a summer wine for the river towns and for charcuterie.
A small production of traditional method sparkling, often Fernão Pires and Arinto, crisp and simple, poured as an aperitif.

exam: Define the style in a breath: light, high acid, low alcohol, a prickle, bottled young; verde means young.
Name the grapes by colour: Alvarinho, Loureiro, Trajadura, Arinto (Pedernã), Avesso and Azal for white; Vinhão for red.
Place Monção e Melgaço on the Minho in the rain shadow and tie Alvarinho to it.
Know the nine sub-regions exist and name the ones the exam uses: Monção e Melgaço, Lima, Baião.
Hold the Spanish pairing: Albariño, Rías Baixas, Condado do Tea across the river.
Know the IGP, Vinho Regional Minho, and the soil, granite.
Explain the high training and why: rain, rot, and a field of maize underneath.

grapes.name: Alvarinho
grapes.styles: The region's serious white, thick-skinned and sure of ripening in Monção e Melgaço: twelve to thirteen per cent, peach, citrus and a stony edge, no spritz, sometimes lees or oak, and able to age a few years.

grapes.name: Loureiro
grapes.styles: The floral workhorse, named for the laurel its scent recalls, at home in the Lima valley: lime blossom, orange peel and bright acidity, the lead grape of most good blends.

grapes.name: Trajadura
grapes.styles: Soft, fuller and lower in acid, the classic partner that rounds Alvarinho and Loureiro; Treixadura across the river.

grapes.name: Arinto
grapes.styles: Called Pedernã here: acidity and citrus for the blends, and the grape that keeps the cheapest wines fresh.

grapes.name: Avesso
grapes.styles: The grape of Baião in the warmer south-east, fuller and more peachy, making the roundest whites of the region and a few varietal wines.

grapes.name: Azal
grapes.styles: A late, high-acid white of Basto and Amarante, lean and green-appled, mostly for blending.

grapes.name: Vinhão
grapes.styles: The red grape, a teinturier with red flesh: opaque purple, foaming, sharp and drying, drunk young and cold from a ceramic bowl with pork; Sousão in the Douro.

grapes.name: Espadeiro
grapes.styles: A pale, fruity red used mostly for the region's rosé.

law.classification: The Região Demarcada dos Vinhos Verdes was created by law in 1908, one of the demarcations that followed the Douro's by a century and a half, and today it is DOC Vinho Verde under its own commission, the CVRVV, with Vinho Regional Minho as the IGP around it. The DOC is divided into nine sub-regions whose names may appear on the label: Monção e Melgaço, Lima, Cávado, Ave, Basto, Sousa, Amarante, Baião and Paiva. The grape list is long, with Alvarinho, Loureiro, Trajadura, Arinto, Avesso and Azal as the whites that matter and Vinhão, Espadeiro, Borraçal and Padeiro among the reds. Alcohol is written into the rules: the plain category is held to a low ceiling that the Alvarinho and sub-region wines may pass. Alvarinho's name was once Monção e Melgaço's alone on a DOC label; Portaria 152/2015 widened the use of the grape's name across the region and left the sub-region its exclusive claim to Vinho Verde Alvarinho until 2021, and Portaria 333/2016 added the optional mention Origem do Alvarinho for its wines.
labels: Young, not green: the wine is meant for the year after harvest.
White, red, rosé; the red is Vinhão and the rosé usually Espadeiro.
A producer's selection, a step above the basic blend, not a legal ageing term.
A selected harvest, vintage dated, with a higher alcohol floor.
Needle: a wine with a prickle of gas, the Vinho Verde style in a word.

tiers: DOC Vinho Verde
The whole demarcated region from the Minho to the Douro, demarcated in 1908: light wines of the listed grapes, the plain category held low in alcohol by rule.
Vinho Verde with a sub-region
One of the nine sub-regions on the label, Monção e Melgaço above all; the wine must come from that sub-region and its recommended grapes and may carry more alcohol than the plain category.
Vinho Verde Alvarinho
The single-varietal wine from Alvarinho, reserved to Monção e Melgaço until the 2015 ordinance's transition ended in 2021; it carries more alcohol than the plain category.
Vinho Verde Espumante
Sparkling wine from the region's grapes, the best by the traditional method.
Vinho Regional Minho
The IGP for the same territory: wider grape list, fuller wines, and the home of many varietal Alvarinhos from outside the sub-region before 2021.

made.viticulture: The old Minho vineyard was a hedge, not a field: vines trained high on granite posts and wires in the ramada, a pergola, or run up trees, the enforcado, around the margins of plots that grew maize and cabbages beneath them. Height kept the fruit in the wind and away from the damp ground, and gave the family its vegetables; it also gave enormous yields and thin, acid wine. Modern vineyards use the cruzeta, a cross-armed post with the vine trained along wires two metres up, or ordinary cordons on lower trellises, with the canopy opened to dry the bunches. Granite and rain still set the rules: mildew and botrytis are constant, spraying is frequent, and the harvest in September is a race between ripeness and the autumn rains. Holdings are tiny, the minifúndio of the north, so co-operatives and big brands buy from thousands of growers. Monção e Melgaço is the exception in every sense: warmer, drier, planted mostly to Alvarinho on terraces and slopes above the river, and picked riper.
made.winemaking: The prickle that defines the wine was once an accident: wines bottled young went through malolactic fermentation in bottle and kept the carbon dioxide. Today the rule allows a measured dose of carbon dioxide at bottling, and nearly every commercial Vinho Verde is made in stainless steel, fermented cold with cultured yeast, malolactic blocked to keep the acidity, and bottled within months with a few grams of residual sugar to soften the edge. Alcohol is kept low by picking early and by the character of the grapes, and the standard category is capped by law. Alvarinho and the better sub-region wines are made like any serious white: riper fruit, no added gas, lees contact for texture and, from some houses, barrel fermentation or a year in old wood. The red Vinhão is fermented fast on its skins, often in the open, and bottled unfiltered so that it foams in the glass. The best sparkling wines use the traditional method.

places.name: Monção e Melgaço
places.note: The north-eastern sub-region along the Minho opposite Galicia, sheltered by the hills of the Peneda so that it is warmer and drier than the coast. It is the home of Alvarinho, the one sub-region the exam asks by name, and the source of the region's fullest and longest-lived whites; the varietal wines that made the grape famous came from here in the 1970s.

places.name: Monção
places.note: The riverside town whose co-operative, the Adega de Monção, and whose manor house Palácio da Brejoeira put varietal Alvarinho on the map; the flat lands near the river and the slopes behind are all Alvarinho.

places.name: Melgaço
places.note: Portugal's northernmost municipality, higher and hillier up the Minho, where the small estates that lead the modern Alvarinho movement are based; the terraces climb towards the Peneda.

places.name: Lima
places.note: The valley of the Lima river around Ponte de Lima, west of Monção, and the heartland of Loureiro: floral, lifted whites, some old pergola vineyards, and a handful of estates making Loureiro with lees and age.

places.name: Cávado and Ave
places.note: The two central sub-regions nearest Braga and the coast, wet and populous, where thousands of small growers feed the co-operatives and the big blends; Loureiro, Arinto and Trajadura whites, with Vinhão for the reds.

places.name: Sousa
places.note: Around Penafiel and Paredes in the south, the base of the region's largest house and its best-known brand; Loureiro, Arinto and Avesso whites and plenty of Vinhão red.

places.name: Basto
places.note: The inland eastern sub-region on the Tâmega around Celorico de Basto, the most continental and the last to pick, where Azal keeps its acidity and the reds are sharp.

places.name: Amarante
places.note: On the Tâmega below the Marão, warmer than the coast, growing Avesso and Azal for fuller whites and Vinhão for red; the town itself is the border town between the Minho and the Douro road.

places.name: Baião
places.note: The south-eastern corner on the Douro's north bank, the warmest and driest sub-region, part schist, and the home of Avesso: the roundest whites in Vinho Verde and the only ones that can read like a Douro white.

places.name: Paiva
places.note: A small sub-region south across the Douro around Castelo de Paiva, better known for red Vinhão than for whites.

places.name: Vinho Regional Minho
places.note: The IGP that shares the DOC's territory: the home of fuller, international-leaning whites and, until the 2021 transition ended, of the varietal Alvarinhos grown outside Monção e Melgaço.

producers.name: Anselmo Mendes
producers.why: The Melgaço house that showed Alvarinho could be serious: single-vineyard, lees-aged and barrel-fermented bottlings that set the grape's benchmark.

producers.name: Quinta de Soalheiro
producers.why: A Melgaço family estate that bottled the first Alvarinho from the municipality in 1982 and became the grape's most widely poured name abroad.

producers.name: Palácio da Brejoeira
producers.why: The Monção manor whose varietal Alvarinho from the 1970s made the grape's reputation before anyone else bottled it.

producers.name: Adega de Monção
producers.why: The Monção co-operative whose Alvarinho and Trajadura blend is the honest, cheap face of the sub-region.

producers.name: Aveleda
producers.why: The Penafiel house in the Sousa sub-region behind Casal Garcia, launched in 1939 and one of the biggest brands of Vinho Verde in the world.

producers.name: Quinta do Ameal
producers.why: A Lima valley estate that proved Loureiro could be made with lees and oak and age for years.

producers.name: Aphros
producers.why: A biodynamic Lima estate known for Loureiro, Vinhão and the region's early pét-nat sparkling wines.

producers.name: Quinta de Covela
producers.why: A Baião estate on the Douro's bank that gave Avesso a serious varietal wine.

terroir.climate: Cool, humid and Atlantic. Weather arrives off the ocean and the rainfall is among the heaviest of any European vineyard, commonly above 1,200 millimetres a year and well beyond that in the hills, much of it in autumn and winter. Winters are mild, summers warm rather than hot, and humidity, mildew and rot are the grower's daily enemies. Inland, up the Minho at Monção and Melgaço, the hills of the Peneda shelter the valley: it is drier and warmer, swings more between day and night, and ripens Alvarinho to twelve or thirteen per cent where the coast struggles past ten.
terroir.soils: Granite almost everywhere, weathered into coarse, sandy, acidic topsoil that drains fast and is poor in nutrients, which is the counterweight to the rain. Towards the south and east, around Baião and Amarante where the region meets the Marão and the Douro, bands of schist appear, and the river valleys carry alluvium. The low fertility and the acidity of the soil are part of why the wines stay light.
terroir.topography: A green, crowded country of hills and river valleys rising from the coast towards the Peneda-Gerês mountains in the north-east and the Serra do Marão in the south-east, which wall it off from the inland. Vineyards run from near sea level to a few hundred metres, nearly all in small family plots on the slopes and valley floors, historically planted around the edges of fields that grew maize beneath them.
terroir.water: The Minho forms the northern border with Galicia; across it lie O Rosal and Condado do Tea of Rías Baixas, and the same grape is Albariño there and Alvarinho here. The Lima, Cávado and Ave run west to the Atlantic, the Sousa and the Paiva into the Douro, and those five rivers give five sub-regions their names; the Tâmega runs through Basto and Amarante to the Douro, which bounds the south at Baião. The ocean keeps the climate mild and wet.

traps: Verde is young, not green: the colour of the wine is not the point, and red Vinho Verde exists.
The spritz is not a sparkling wine; espumante is a separate category made by the traditional method.
Alvarinho is Albariño, not Loureiro; Loureiro is Loureira in Galicia and Trajadura is Treixadura.
Vinhão is Sousão in the Douro: one teinturier grape, two names.
The region's IGP is Minho, not Vinho Verde; the sub-region is Monção e Melgaço, not Monção alone.

The old note that Alvarinho may only be labelled from Monção e Melgaço is out of date: the 2015 ordinance opened the grape's name to the region, with the sub-region's exclusivity on the varietal label ending with the 2021 transition.

wines.note: Pale, light at nine to eleven per cent, bone dry to just off dry, green apple, lime and a faint prickle; serve very cold with grilled sardines, salt cod fritters, clams or oysters. The glass pour and the wine most people mean by the name.

The serious tier: fuller, twelve to thirteen per cent, peach, grapefruit and wet stone, no spritz, often with lees contact and sometimes a little oak; good with richer fish, roast chicken and Asian food, and it keeps for several years.
wines.style: Vinho Verde Alvarinho and Monção e Melgaço

wines.note: A varietal from the Lima valley and elsewhere: floral, laurel and citrus, light and lifted, a fine aperitif and a match for ceviche and salads.
Vinhão's wine, opaque purple with a pink foam, tart and tannic, served chilled in a bowl with rojões, fried pork, in its own tavernas; a trivia point for the exam and a shock for an unprepared guest.
Rosés from Espadeiro and Vinhão, and sparkling wines, the best by the traditional method, from Alvarinho or Loureiro, both small categories that show the region's acidity to advantage.
